The official British statement shows
that the Zeppelins penetrated to the
heart of industrial England. Lincoln-
shire is on the east coast. Its south-
ern boundary is seventy-five miles
north of London. Leicestershire ad-
joins it to the southwest. Derby-
shire is northwest of Leicestershire
and Staffordshire is to the west of
Derbyshire. These counties comprise
a strip of territory in mid-England,
extending more than 100 miles from
the North Sea. Staffordshire and
Derbyshire have important manufac-
turing interests. The other counties
are given over largely to agriculture.

WARNING IN PARIS.
[BY A. F. DAY WIRE)

PARIS, Feb. 1.—A Zeppelin started
in the dérection of Paris last night at
9:45 o'clock. A warning was sent
out from Compiegne that a German
airship had been sighted in move-
ment. The Military Governor of Paris
gave orders that preparations be
made to give the alarm if neces-
sary. When the Zeppelin, however,
got into the fleld of the searchlights
on the French front it turned back
and is supposed to have abandoned a
projected raid.

ef the campaign for the renomination

FEATURES OF SETTLEMENT.

The principal features of the memo-
randum of set‘ ement in the Lusitania
dispute are:

Germany sank the Lusitania as a
reprisal, recognized as legitimate by
international law, upon Great Britain
in retaliation for the illegal and in-
— 4 starvation blockade of Ger-

Germany was shocked by the fact

innocent American citizens and deep-
ly regrets the occurrence,

Germany recognizes that while the
sinking of a British vessel was a
legitimate reprisal, the resultant sac-
rifice of the lives of innocent neutrals
was an illegal and unjustifiable act.

y, out of friendship for the
United States, abandoned this form of

henceforth Americans traveling on
peaceful liners shoul be safe from
attack without provision for their
safety.

Germany, realizing that the killing
of the 115 American citizens on the
Lusitanii was illegal, is ready to
indemnities for the loss of these lives
and recommends that the amount of
the reparation be fixed by further ne-
gotiation.

ASHINGTON, Feb. 12 The
possibility that a German sub-
marine accompanied the cap-

tured British liner Appam across the
Atlantic and was preparing to operate
off the American coast aroused much
interest among navy officials here.

If, as navy officials have reason
to believe, Germany recentiy has de-
veloped submersibles of a thousand
tons displacement or more, a trans-
Atlantic voyage could be made with-
out great hardship.

Navy officers generally were skep-
tical of the reports, however, al-
though, it was recalied, that the flood
of American-made munitions to the
allied powers probabiy would begin
to reach its full proportion within the
next few months, ft!viting unusual
efforts by the Teutonic naval forces.

is her torpedoes and no submersipie
can carry more than half a dozen.

SEPARATE PEACE OPFER
IS DENIED BY ENGLAND.

{BY ATLANTIC CABLE AND A.

ONDON, Feb. 1.—Official denial
was made here today of reports
attributed to German sources

That England Intends to abandon her

Alles and has made peace overtures
to Germany. The statement follows:
“The German Chancellor has stated
4 ts compelling her al-
refrain from entering upon any
peace movements. This statement,
which our allies know to be untrue,

was made for the purpose of injuring
England in the eyes of neutrals.

o our allies, on the other hand,
we hear that insidious and untrue
reports are being circulated from
German sources that England in-
tends to abandon them and has even
made peace overtures to Germany
which have been refused.

“The two statements together are
ustration of how un-
are.

troversies which have arisen on the |
Other side of the water—abandon its
habitual and traditional policy and
deliberately engage in the conflict
which is now engulfing the rest of
the world. I do not know what the
standards of citizenship of these gen-
tlemen may be. I only know that I,
ol one, subscribe to those

dard
“I believe that I more truly speak

the spirit of America when I say that“

spirit is a spirit of peace. Why, no

Voice has ever come to any public}

man more audibly, more unmistak-
ably, than the voice of this great peo-
ple has come to me, bearing this im-
pressive lesson:

We are counting upon you to
keep this country out of war.’

“And I call you to witness, my fel-
low-countrymen, that I have spent
every thought and energy that has been
vouchsafead me in order to keep this
country out of war. It cannot be dis-
closed now, perhaps it can never be
disclosed, how anxious and how dim-
cult that task has been, but my heart
has been in it. I have not grudged a

single burden that has been thrown}

upon me with that end in view, for 1
knew that not only my own heart,
but the heart of all America was in
the cause of peace.

“And yet, my fellow-citizens, there
are some men among us preachirg
peace who go much further than 1
can go. Not further than I can go
in the sentiment of peace; not fur-
ther than peace warrants them in. go-
ing in * ting the desire and
sentiment America; but further
than I can follow them; further, I
believe, than you can follow them, in
preaching the doctrine of peace at any
price in any circumstances. There
is a price which is too great to pay
for peace, and that price can be put
in one word. One cannot pay the price
of self-respect. One cannot pay the
price of duties abdicated, of glorious
opportunities neglected, of character,
national character, vindicated and
exemp in action. America has a
character as distinct as the character
of any individual among us. We read
that character in every page of her
singular and glorious history. We be-
lleve that that character is written in
invisible signs, which, nevertheless,

our spirits can decipher upon the very p

folds of the flag which is the emblem
of our national life. ‘

“The gentlemen, out and out pa-
cificists, are making one fundamental
mistake. That is not a mistake about
the sentiments of America, but a mis-
take about the circumstances of the
world. America does not constitute
the world. In many of her sentiments
and predilections she does not repre-
sent or influence the world.

{ dangers to our peace do not
come any longer from within our own
borders. I could not have said that
a few months ©. Passion was astir
in this country. There was a clash of
sympathies and heat of passion which
made our air tense and made men
hold their breath for fear some of our
fellow-countrymen would forget that
their first loyalty was to America and
their second loyalty only to the
ancient affections which bound them,
and honorably bound them. to some
older country and polity. But those
Jangers have passed. America has re-
gained her eelf- on. Men are
now ready to feel and to act in com-
mon in the great cause of the national
life, an@ no influence within America
is going to disturb the peace of Amer-

“Rut America cannot be an ostrich
with {te head in the sand. America
cannot shut itself out from the rest
of the world. because all the dangers
at this present moment, and they are
many, come from her contacts with
the rest of the world. And those con-
tacts are going to be largely deter-
mined by other nations and not deter-
mined by ourselves.

DANGER FROM OUTSIDE.

“Do you want it to be only a voice

these breaches of international] law

ring, should touc hthe v vital in-

MILITIA BILL:
CAUSES A ROW.

Secretary Garrison in Breach

with National Guard.

Declares System a Failure and
Menace to Safety.

We're at Parting of the Ways,
Says Department Head.

(BY A P. NIGHT WIRE. ]

WASHINGTON, Feb. 1.—Secretary
Garrison and the Executive Commit-
tee of the National Guard Association
came to a breach today over the ad-
ministration’s plan for a continental
army instead of organized militia as
the nation’s main reliance in war
time.

Before the Senate and House mill-
tary committees, members of the
guardsmen's committee, headed by
Adjt.-Gen. Foster of Florida, declared
the continental army scheme im-
practical” and contended for fed-
eralization of the National Guard by
Congressional action. Compensation
guardsmen by the Federal
government for actual services
rendered was urged, although Gen.
Foster objected to designating as
a “militia pay proposal.

A letter from Secretary Garrison to
Chairman Chamberlain of the Senate
committee, disapproving the Sena-
tor’s mili bill, was made public at
the War partment. After declarin
that the guardsmen always have st
in the way of the organization of a
urely Federal volunteer foree on
sound lines, Mr. n wrote:

“Having arrived at a consideration
involving pay of the National G
we have come to the final parting o
the ways. The passage of such a
measure would fully and irretrievably
commit us to a system that has ut-
terly falled in the past, which
menaces our safety now; a system in
which the people justly have no con-

fidence.
“If we put the militia
firmly in the saddle as is contem-

plated in this bill, the opportunity
for adopting a sound military policy

for the nation will have passed beyond“

recall.”

PROPOSALS WELL RECEIVED.

The proposals of the guardsmen
were well received in both commit-
tees. They were invited by the Sen-
ate committee to draft their plan in
the form of a bill, and several mem-
bers of the House committee took oc-
casion to con tulate Gen. Foster
and Maj.-Gen. John R. O’Ryan, of the
New York National Guard, who aiso
spoke of the showing they had made
in behalf of the State troops.

Gens. Foster and O'Ryan and other
National Guard officers present, in-
cluding Gen. W. J. Stewart of Penn-
syivania, president of the National
Guard Association; Gen. A. B. Critch-
feld of Ohio, and Gen. W. F. Sad-
ler, Jr., of New Jersey, were agreed
that there was no constitutional bar-
rier to a very complete degree of Fed-
eral control over the National Guard.
Congress never had fully used its
power in that direction, they de-
clared,

Only the extraterritorial use of
the State. forces without their con-
sent was denied the Federal govern-
ment by the Constitution, Gen O' Ryan
asserted, and in this, virtually all
countries were alike. The imperial!
army of Japan could not be sent
abroad on any but a defensive move-
ment except when they volunteered,
he said, and the same was true in
the much-discussed niilitia system of
Switzerland and Australia.

GEN. FOSTER’S VIEW.

Discussing the question of com-
— the militia, Gen. Foster
said:

“The National Guard does not ask
a dollar from the public this year
for which it cannot give à full meas-
ure of service in return. In the first
place, it should be considered that
under any system of volunteer mill-
tary service the government must pay
for such service, and that whether
this cost takes the form of expendi-
tures to train fit soldiers for active
duty or is pajd in bounty and pen-,
sions to compensate for casualties at-
tributable to the incompetefcy of
unpreparedness is a matter of
choice—but with all argument for
economy favoring the first named.”

Gen. Foster declared the War De-
Partment had favored militia com-
pensation legislation all along, al-
though the present Secretary had not
specifically recommended passage of
such acts. Without knowledge of the
letter issued by Secretary Garrison,

n. Foster read a report of the con-
ference between his committee and
the Secretary last October, where the
administration plans had been dis-

cussed,

report had been dictated by
he sald, and was as fol-

“The final matter that remains in
my memory that has not been alluded
to I propose to state exactly in the
form which it occurred so that there

Supposing the

Senator Chamberlain said:

“Just as soon as we complete con-
sideration of the regular establishment
we are estopped from proceeding to
establish a sound system of citizen
soldiers by the existence of a force
that we cannot count upon, either for
Peace training or war employment,
yet having such influence that we have
not béen able te disregard it and pro-
ceed to the organization of a proper
force of trained citizenry on a strictly
Federal basis

“After the -American War
demonstrated the utter weakness of
our military policy an effort was made
to secure the enactment of a Federal
volunteer law under which the army
could be directly organized and em-
ployed by the government. The wis-
dom of stich a measure needed no ar-
gument; but the active opposition of
some influential members of the or-
ganized militia was such as to keep
this measure pending for years.
Finally, when it was passed, they suc-
ceeded in having injected into it a
provision for the acceptance of or-
ganized militia as volunteers. The in-
tent and purpose of these provisions
was to require the Federal govern-
ment to employ an uncertain force of
organized militia before proceeding to
Organize the national army of volun-
teers. Under such a system mobiliza-
tion for war will be again attended
with confusion, delay and embafrass-
ment, and campaigns will probably be
attended with disaster.”

FOR RESERVE ENGINEERS.
{BY A. Fb. DAY WIRE.)

NEW YORK. Feb. 1.— Plans for
providing the United States army
with a reserve corps of at least 80,000
civilian engineers for coast and other
defense work in time of war have
been approved, it was announced here
tonight by the American Society of
Civil Engineers, the American Insti-
tute of Mining Engineers, the Amer-
ican Society of Mechanical neers
and the American Institute Elec-
trical Engineers.

Maj.-Gen, Leonard Wood will direct
the organization of the corps, which is
to have ita headquarters in Pittsburgh,
Pa. A series of seven lectures, pre-
paratory to permanent organization,
will be delivered by army officers, be-
ginning February 14,

In Une with President Wilson's sug-
gestions for national defense, the
idea is that in case of emergency the
civilian engineers could be pressed
into service and release the regular
army engineers on duty in the field.

CHINESE INSURGENTS
CROSS GREAT WALL.

[BY ATLANTIC CABLE AND A. P.)

LONDON, Feb. 1—The Mongolian
insurgents have crossed the great wall
of China and an advance guard of
2000 is besieging the city of Da Tum
Fa, according to a dispatch from
Mukden forwarded by Reuter's corre
spondent at Petrograd.

Dispatches from Mukden yesterday
reported that the Mongolian in-
surgents had been heavily reinforced
and were marching toward Peking.
No mention was made of their having
erossed the Mongolian border, which,
at its nearest poft to Peking, is ap-
proximately 200 miles from that city.

ORANGE PICKING ON.

Trees in Good Condition to Stand a

(BY DIRECT WIRB—EXCLU¥IVE DIAPATCH. }
POMONA, Feb. 1.—The tempera-
ture ranged from 27 deg. to 29 deg.
this morning. At 2 o’clock a slight
breeze from the northeast caused it
to go up about 3 deg. Before 4
o'clock there was very little firing.
Some was done in the San Dimas
district to protect the lemon buds,
but the orange growers did nothing
more than light their border rows.
This was the first day of real orange
picking in the valley. It is estimated
that more than twenty care of navels
were hurried into the packing-houses
today.
There is very little danger of dam-
age by cold. The cold snap early in
the season drove the sap out of the
leaves and twigs from the leaves into
the trunk of the trees. The fruit is
well developed and it would take a
low temperature, sustained for sev-
eral hours, to do any noticeable dam-
age. It is slightly warmer tonight.

ASH-REGISTER
SUIT DISMISSED.

DEFENDANT AGREES TO DE-
MAND OF THE GOVERNMENT.

Decree Enjoins Company from In-
terfering in Any Manner with
Competitors and Assesses the
Costs of the Case, Forty Thousand
Dollars, on the Dayton Concern.

{BY A. r. DAY wn!

CINCINNATI (0.) Feb. 1.—Prac-
tically every change asked for by the
United States government in its ac-
tion against the National Cash Reg-
ister Company of Dayton, O., under
the civil section of the Sherman anti-
trust law, was agreed to by the de-
fendants today, when a consent-
agreement was filed by attorneys for
the defendants and the government
in the United States District Court.

The government's litigation against
John H. Patterson and the other
twenty-six officials and former offi-
cials of the National Cash Register
Company under the criminal section
of the Sherman law was dismissed by
the court, the costs being assessed
against the defendants, These costs
will amount to about $40,000.

These defendants were convicted
in the lower court, but the Circuit
Court of Appeals reversed the deci-
sien and remanded the case back to
the trial court.

THINGS NOT TO DO.

The decree in the civil suit enjoins
the National Cash Register Company
from:

Restraining interstate commerce,

Persuading purchasers of other
makes of registers to break or re-
pudiate their contracts.

Maintaining a system of espionage
upon competitors.

Tilegally securing competitors’
business secrets,

Inducing men to leave competitors’

service.

Copying designs of rival makers
of registers in order to deceive the
buyers.

Maintaining “knock-out men.“

Discrediting competitors’ standing.

Intimidating competitors by threats
of patent infringement suits and ac-
quiring ownership of the business,
patents or plants or competitors
without the consent of the court and
the approval of the Attorney General.

Under the terms of the decree the
Federal Court will retain jurisdiction
over the case for the purpose of en-
forcing the injunction.

The dismissal of the criminal case
follows the reversal of the conviction
of President Patterson and his asso-
clates by the United States Circult
Court of Appeals and the refusal of
the Supreme Court to review the case.
Mr. Patterson was sentenced to serve
a vear in prison and pay a fine of
$5000, while the twenty-three other
defendants received prison sentences
or fines.

[BY A. F. DAY WIRE)

KANSAS CITY (Mo.) Feb. 1.—Fire
broke out at 1:40 p.m. today in the
Western Union Telegraph Company's
three-story buflding at Seventh and
Main streets. Many operators were
forced to leave the working rooms on
the upper floors by means of fire es-
capes.

The fire broke out on the second
floor and endangered the lives of 800
employees at work in the operating-
room, fifty of whom were carried
down fire escapes to safety. At 2
o'clock the blaze was under control
and all employees had been accounted
safe.

The cause of the fire is unknown.

Entrance to the operating-room on
the third floor is through a hall lead-
ing down two long flights of stairs to
the street. When the operators en-
tered this hall a burst of fame met
them. Practically all of the employees
were forced to descend on the fire es-
capes.

Officials of the company said only
the constant practice of a fire drin
saved the lives of many employees,

it was near daylight today when she
appeared between the capes. She did
not sight a single British or French
man-of-war from the time she parted
company with the Moewe until she

CLEAN BILL OF HEALTH.

When the Appam dropped anchor
in Hampton Roads she was boarded
by the quarantine officer, Dr. H. W.
McCaffery, and given a clean bill of
health. Soon afterwards Lieut. Berge
came ashore and called upon German
Consul Von Shilling and together they
went to the office of Col. Haynes, com-
mandant of Fort Monroe, to pay an
official call. The commander of the
prize then reported by telephone the
arrival of the vessel to Collector Ham-
ilton of the Norfolk-Newport News
district, and later he came to Norfolk
and made a statement of facts to Mr,
Hamilton for transmission to the
ashington officials.

Just what the commander sald to
the collector about the treatment he
desired from the United States has
not been revealed and will not be until
Washington has passed on the case.
Mr. Hamilton accepted his word as a
naval officer that he would not at-
tempt to move the liner from her
anchorage, or permit anyone to come
ashore pending further instructions.

Lieut. Berge said that the Appam
arrived short of both fuel and provi-
sions and that there was not enough
food aboard to last through tomorrow.
Mr. Hamilton gave permission to take
on a quantity of stores tonight.

WOMEN AND CHILDREN.

Among those aboard are fifteen
women and many children, the exact
number of which has not been deter-
mined.

Sir Edward Meriwether, Governor
of Sierra Leone, a British province in
West Africa, and his wife are pas-
sengers. There are also several of-
ficers of the British army and navy.
Others included Fred James, Secre-
tary-Administrator of Nigeria, who is
a relative of Lord Decies.

The masters of all of the vessels
captured are on the Appam except the
captain of the Clan MacTavish, who
with most of the members of his crew
probably were taken aboard the
Moewe.

The captured skippers. are H. G.
Harrison of the Appam; Ralph T.
Yeates of the Author; David Barton
of the Corbridge; Robert Reid of the
Adrladne: John Brockett of the Dro-
monby; John P. Jones of the Far-
ringford,

Collector Hamilton was in com-
munication by telephone today with
Treasury Department officials, to
whom he made a full statement of
the facts as resented to him by
Lieut. Berge. onight he sent a long
written statement to the department

Lieut. Berge refused to give any,in-
formation to any newspaper men and
would permit none of them to come
aboard while the status of the vessel
remained undetermined. He refused
to identify himself other than to say
he was a lieutenant in the naval re-
serve and formerly was master of a
German merchant vessel. During his
interview with Collector Hamilton he
remarked that many times he had
been in the Norfolk customhouse to
enter and clear vessels engaged in
trade. He did not mention the names
of these vessels, however.

From .all reports there was great
excitement aboard the Appam during
the battle between the Moewe and the
Clan MacTavish. although the, liner
was about ten miles away at the time.
The Clan MacTavish was armed with
only one or two small guns for de-
fensive purposes, but her encounter
with the Moewe was described as an
“exciting combat.” The fact that the
Moewe sustained no damage in the
fight is accepted-as indicating that her
guns were of larger caliber and long-
er range, as the Clan MacTavish was
sunk and fifteen men killed and at
least three wounded.

RUMOR CURRENT.

A rumor was current shortiv after
the Appam’s arrival here that she had
heen captured by a submarine. Then
when the facts were known another
report was circulated that a German
submarine had convoved the liner
across the ocean. Lieut. Berge did
not confirm this and little credence
was given it by port officials. Hoy-
ever, the British authorities here have
advised merchant vessels of the allies
in Hampton Roads to stay in port un-
tin the situation clears. No ehips
were due to sail today, but several had
expected to put to sea early tomorrow.

Lleut. Berge, a heavy-set German
soldier with reddish mustache and
imperial, gave Collector Hamilton no
more information than he considered

disclose the identity of the Moewe,
nor the name of her commander. but
he admitted that he himself had been
merely a subordinate officer on the
raider. He supplied no detafls of the
capture of the vessels taken by the
Moewe, firmly refusing to be cross-
examined.

VILLA IN ROLE

OF HOLD-UP MAN.

Stops Mexican Central Train|

with a Few Followers.

Then Orders the Killing of
Cen. Tomas Ornelas.

Personally Directs Looting and
Robs Passengers.

[BY 4. F. NIGHT WIRE.)

EL PASO (Tex.) Feb. 1.—Francisco
Villa, with less than 100 followers.
held up a south-bound Mexican Cen-
tral passenger train a few miles
north of Chihuahua City yesterday

and ordered the killing of Gen. Tomas

Ornelas, according to advices from

Chihuahua City, received today by

Gen. Gavira, Mexican commandant at
Juarez.
Gen. Gavira was also advised that

Villa directed the looting of

the train robbery of the passen-
Gers. It is said that there were no
Americans aboard. After the train

nad been looted, Villa, it was said, per-
| mitted it to proceed. One report was
| that Villa and his band afterward left

for the hills of Western Chihuahua,
while another said he departed in the

— of Ojinaga, opposite Presidio,

Gen. Luis Herrera reported to the
Mexicon Consulate here that a detach-
ment of Mexican troops had taken up
the trail of Villa at Sauz, where the
hold-up and killing of Ornelas took
Place. The report added that Villa
and his band, mounted to good horses
Stolen from the Hearst ranch at Ba-
bricora, had secured a good start upon
‘their pursuers.

It was established that among the

gers on the train robbed by
ila were Jose Bovio, Italian, and
Joseph Meyer.

| FORESEES NO STRIFE

AMONG COAL MINERS.

(BY A. P. NIGHT WIRE.)

INDIANAPOLIS, Feb. 1.—The bien-
nial convention of the Unite Mine
Workers’ of America adjourne today
to meet in Indianapolis in 1918, and
the attention of the international offi-
cers will not be concentrated in hav-
ing written into new contracts the
plans adopted by the delegates repre-
senting nearly 400,000 anthracite and
bituminous miners.

The next step will be the joint
interstate conference of operators and
miners at Mobile next week, at which
an effort will be made to agree upon
a basis wage scale for Western Penn-
syivania, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois,
which will also be the basis for the
working out of wage agreements in
other soft coal flelds of the country.

On February 21 anthracite oper-
ators and mine workers will meet in
New York to try to agree on a new
contract to take the place of the four-
year agreement which expires March
31. Both the officers of the union and
the delegates themselves believe that
agreements will be reached without
interference with the coal mining in-
dustry.

Before adjourning President White
announced that he had decided to
stand as a candidate for re-election
next December. Officers are elected by
referendum.

Edward Dobbins, Belleville, III.,

were elected delegates to the conven-
tion of the Western Federation of
Miners.

INCREASED PAY
FOR LEAD MINERS.

{BY A. v. DAY WIRE]

KELLOGG (Idaho) Feb. 1.—One
thousand miners employed by the
Bunker Hill and Sullivan, the Cale-
donia, Ontario and Sierra Nevada
mines here will recover a bonus of
50 cents the shift when the January
pay checks are made out, according
to an announcement posted at the
mines today

When lead is quoted at $5. to $5.50
the miners will receive a bonus of 25
cents the shift. Lead at $5.50 to $6
will mean a bonus of 50 cents and
lead at better than $6 means a bonus

lead in January was $5.94.
The miners here have been recetv-
ing $3 a day.

TEN PER CENT. RAISE :
FOR STEEL WORKERS.

(BY A. F. DAY

NEW YORK, Feb. 1.—The United
States Steel Corporation put into ef-
fect today an advance of 10 per cent.
in the wages of its employees. It is
estimated that the increase will add
to the corporation’s annual pay roll
and that it will affect about 250,000
men. -Of this number approximately

tofore has been between 19 and 20
cents an hour. They will receive here-
after 21 to 22 cents an hour.

FEAR SHE DROWNED.

“Girl who Never had a Chance,” Es-
| ‘caping from Whittier in Night
of Storm, may Have Dost Her
Lite in the Raging San
Gabriel River.

The fate of Miss Mamie Swezea,
the girl who never had a chance, is
worrying the Juvenile Court. She es-
caped from Whittier school on a
stormy night, and the San Gabriel
River lay between Whittier and Los
Angeles, where it is believed she would
head.

The suspicion that she was drowned
is strengthened by the fact that a
fragment. of her clothing was found
by searchere on the river bank, caught
by the bushes.

No other indication of her fate has
reached the probation office, which
has sent out the alarm.

ON A POINT OF LAW.

If a Woman’s Mind was Affected by
Injury She is Incompetent to Sue,
Pieads Railway’s Attorney.
Court Halts to Consider
Doctor’s Testimony.

A novel eftuation arose yesterday
in the trial of the $10,000 damage
suit of Mrs. Mattie Darrah against the
Los Angeles Railway Company, grow-
ing out of injuries she sustained while
alighting from a car. Dr. C. L. Rey-
nolds, called as an expert, stated that
in his opinion the injuries she re-
ceived affected her mind.

Attorney Sterry, representing the
company, raised the point that if her
mind is unbalanced, she could not
maintain the suit.

Judge Myers dismissed the jury and
stated the case ought not to proceed
further unless a guardian was ap-
pointed or it was fully determined
Mrs. Darrah is competent. It was de-
cided that Mr. Darrah should be ap-
pointed guardian. When this has
been done the case will proceed. At-
torney Green represents Mrs. Darrah.

i ALTS TRAIN:
7 DROPS DEAD.

Raitroad Man Stricken as He
‘Runs to Flag Cars Going
on Open Switch.

Running to flag a train before
it should reach an open switch,
Charles E. Park, a passenger
brakeman of the Southern Pa-
cific, dropped dead from heart.
failure yesterday morning near
Indio. The engineer saw him
fall and stopped. Brother train-
men rushed to pick him up, but
death had been instantaneous.

Mr. Park lived at No. 3030

Budiong avenue, this city, and

had resided here for thirteen
years. He was a Shriner, a
member of the Knights of Pyth-
las, Royal Arcanum and Broth-
erhood of Railway Trainmen.
He was 57 years old and had
been in the railroad business
since he was 15.

“Too Many Preachers,” He

PLUCKY PASTOR
‘BREAKS STONES.

Turns Day Laborer as Work in
Ministry Fails Him.

Well-known Churchman’s Mak-
ing Two-sixty a Day.

Says; Pays Too Low.”

livelihood and provide for his family
as a minister of the gospel, Rev. An-
drew G. C. Brown, 62 years old, whose
wife and three children live at No.
1060 West Thirty-first street in this
city, said yesterday he has found it
necessary to accept work as a day la-
borer, breaking stone at the county
rock camp No. 3, about two miles
from Claremont, and on the State
Highway.

Mr. Brown, who is a graduate of
McCormack Theological Seminary,
Chicago, and his family came to Cali-
fornia from the East about ten years
ago and until two years ago he was
in charge of different Methodist
churches in several small towns near
Los Angeles. In 1914 he gave up the
Pastorate of a church at Sultana,
near Fresno, because of ‘ill-health
and his inability to obtain a satisfac-
tory income, he said yesterday,

For weeks he sought another
charge in vain and finally when his
resources were exhausted, he had to
seek employment in other fields.
After holding several temporary posi-
tions he went to work recently at the
rock camp, where he swings a heavy
hammer from eight to ten hours a
day for wages that average less than
$50 a month.

HE’S CONTENT.

He is apparently contented and says
he will continue his work as a laborer
until he secures a new pastorate.
Mrs. Brown, the wife of the minister,
two pretty daughters, whose ages are
and 11 years, respectively, and a
son, 14 years old, are spending their
time at the family residence in this
city while Mr. Brown is at the rock
camp.

According 40 the other laborers Mr.
Brown is the most popular man in
the gang, which numbers about 160.
Every Sunday morning he preaches
sermon at the camp. ;

“After coming to Los Angeles I dis-
covered there were too many ministers
in Southern California,” Mr. Brown
said yesterday. “My income from
some of my charges was so low I could
not provide for my family and had to
seek a means of livelihood in other.
fields. For days and weeks I searched
for some kind of lucrative employ-
ment, but the best I could find was
work at the rock camp.

TWO-SIXTY A DAY.

“The ordeal Was hard for the first
few days, but I was determined not
to lose out despite the fact I saw
others who were apparently strong
men give up in despair. The camp is
a fine place for unemployed men who
are willing and able to work. Last
Saturday night I was very happy when
I received a check in Claremont for
$26.10, my wages for ten days’ work.

“There are more than 150 men at
the camp and all of them seem to be
contented because they are working
and able to provide for those de-
pendent upon them. The county offi-
clals make it easy for some men to
get employment by advancing their
car fare to the camp from distant
points and then holding it out of
their wages. The sleeping quarters.
are clean and well heated and the
food served is much better than any
T have had at railroad or lumber

camps.

“I am not too good for manual labor
and it is my duty to my family and
myself to swing the hammer when
business is dull in the ministry and
there is no other opportunity for ob-
taining an income.

AERONAUTICAL DIVISION
FOR THE NAVAL MILITIA.

II. WOODBINE of the second
battalion of the Naval Militia of
California, was authorized last night
in a telegram from Adjt.-Gen. Thomas
to muster in an aeronautical section
at once and attach it to the Los An-
geles division of the naval militia with
Ensign Frank Simpson in command.
This plan is part of a genera] move-
ment throughout the United States to
train men for aviation work to be
prepared to aid in the country’s de-
fenses in the event of war, acco
to Lieut. Woodbine who said las
night the school of instruction will
open at Griffith Park next Sunday.

The embryo aviators will use the
$7500 biplane presented last week to
the naval militia by Glenn H. Martin,
who says he will give the students
‘several lectures at the Armory and
aid them in their flights,

It is proposed by local aviators and
others interested in the movement to
train members of the naval militia in
the art of aerial warfare, that $10,000
be raised by popular subscriptions for
purchasing the necessary equipment
and defraying other expenses. Part
of this proposed fund was recently |
subscribed by the Aero Club "|

America.

According to a telegram received last
night by Lieut. Woodbine from Alan
R. Hawley, president of the Aero
Club, a check for $1960 for the Los
Angeles naval miliitia has been sent!
to the Aero Club and will be forwarded
to this city.

The telegram that immediate
preparations should begin all over the
country to train ‘an army of 6000
aviators is as follows:

“Your telegram received, your pub-
lic spiritedness appreciated and check
for $1950 is being malled to Aero
Club of America. I believe your pub-
lic-spirited citizens will contribute

TWO WIVES OR
NAME-DOUBLE?

Turns on Strange Points.

Priest Uncertain of Identity of
Man He Married.

Photograph of Girl Killed in
| Wreck an Exhibit,

Did George C. Norman, son of .
wealthy New York manufacturer,
have more than one wife?

Upon this question apparently turns
his conviction or acquittal on the
charge of having obtained $7000 un-
der false pretenses from the Pacific
Electric Railway on the representa-
tion that Jeannette Teresa Josephson,
who was killed in the Vineyard Sta-
tion wreck on July 13, 1913, was his
legal spouse.

The case was called yesterday morm-
ing in Judge Willies court. The @e-
fendant, accompanied by his attorneya,
John D. Fredericks and Byron Han-
na, did not appear worried. Deputy
District Attorney Doran, assisted by
Deputies Woolwine and Selph, handled
the prosecution.

An effort was made to identify Nor-
man, who has a wife and son resid-
ing in New York, with Norman, the
man who had a wife killed in the
wreck, in which he, too, was hurt and
received $1500 in settlement of his
personal claims from the railway
company. Every minute technicality
was developed by the defense to ex-
clude any damaging testimony
this line.

TWICE MARRIED? ;

Norman was positively identified as
the person who had received the
money for the death of a beautiful
young girl, said to have been his
bride at the time of the accident. The
prosecution then introduced
James Prendergast of Kingston, N. F.,
who was expected to testify that on
September 4, 1904, he had married
the defendant to Mias Elizabeth Morse,
in St. Cecilia's Church, New York

Father Prendergast was not posi-
tive in his personal identifigation, not
having seen Mr. Norman for more
than ten years. He stated that he
had talked to the defendant's wife re-
cently and that she had informed him
that George C. Norman is her husband
and that her son, 7 years old, is the.
son of the defendant. In addition to
this, he produced the church records,
showing that a marriage had occurred
between the persons named.

Complaints that Romolo Corti.
who, with G. W. Cockley, is being
held here on Salt Lake charges of
having used the mails in a scheme
to Gefraud, formerly operated in
dubious stocks on a large scale in
this city, San Francisco and other

Pacific Coast cities, were made yes-
terday to Postoffice Inspector War-

ren.

As far back as the early part of
1906, according to complainants, Cor-
tl, who then advertisea himself, it
is stated, as Romulus Corti, with of-
fices in the Italian-American Bank
Buliding, San Francisco, sold stock
in the Tonopah-Ajax Mining Com-
pany, and the Consolidated Goldfield
Bullfrog Mining Company, which
were alleged to have been incor-
porated under the laws of the then
territory of Arizona. A query to the
Secretary of State of Arizona, shows
Mr. Warren states, that neither com-
pany was ever incorporated in that

The stock was sold at from 10 to
25 cents a share, and an Italian, A.
Venzula, who now lives at No. 146
Clarence street, this city, yesterday
called on I r ren
showed certificates calling for 250
shares in the two companies, for
which to

Vensula was a resident of West Vir-
ginia. He alleges that a number of
his compatriots invested in the stock
as the result of Corti’s activities.

It is alleged
earthquake and fire in San Francisco,
Corti transferred his business to Los
Angeles, where he was engaged for
some time in exploiting various min-
ing properties of more or less dubious
value. Inspector Warren is now in-
vestigating this end of the case. This
was before Corti met Cockley, the
pair drifting together in Chicago,
where Cockley had lost all of his
money in a real estate transaction,
after his retirement from the railway
mail service.

Neither man has been able as yet
to get bond, although when it was
fixed by United States Commissioner
Hammack, Saturday, Cockley de-
clared he would have no difficulty in
furnishing surety.

It is understood that both prisoners
will put up a fight against their ex-
tradition to Utah, alleging that at the
time stock was sold in the Idaho
Bonanza Mining Company, Corti had
secured an extension of the option
given by the administrator of the
Petrovini estate, in Custer county,
Idaho, and had turned over his in-
terests to the corporation, in return
for 995,000 shares of the capital
stock. On the other hand, it is
claimed by the government, that
whatever extension of option had
been granted Corti by the representa-
tive of the Petrovini estate, that it
was done, the show, without
the consent of the courts of Custer
county, through which the appoint-
ment of administrator had been made.

Southland Road Conditions are
Somewhat Improved.

Marooned motorists between Los
Angeles and San Diego are gathering
at Oceanside and preparing to spend
the remainder of the week there un-
less assistance reaches them shortly,
according to a report received yester-
day by officials of the Automobile Club
of Southern California. A “sea-go-
ing” scout car is to be fitted up for

tion.
It is believed that Police Judge

from Caraiff to Oceanside, although
he could not be located yesterday by
family, friends or the Auto Club. The
only statement secured in Oceanside
was to the effect that food is still

holding out. At Cardiff and Del Mar

© situation is not so optimistic. Un-
til the road is opened from Del Mar
to San Diego, there is no hope of the
stranded ones moving more than a
few miles in any direction.

Although Oceanside residents are
now enabled to reach Hsecondido, ac-
cording to a report from Merrill Bro-
thers’ Auto Inn, to the club, this will
avail them nothing, as Escondido is
storm-bound, so far as highways are
concerned.

ROAD BULLETIN.

Following is the road bulletin issued
yesterday by the Automobile Club:

Ridge Route to Bakersfield—This
road will be closed today both from
the ranch end and from the
south. It will be opened tomorrow,
but will be found heavy with mud for
a few days at southern end.

Reach Bakersfield via Bouquet Can-
yon, Elizabeth Lake, Neenac, Balley’s
ranch, and thence over the Tejon Pass.
Motorists should get in Wuch with Au-
tomobile Club Representative Forker
at Board of Trade rooms in Bakers-
Geld before attempting this road.

Mint Canyon—This is passable to-
day, although the first four miles out
of Saugus is extremely muddy with
deep ruts. After crossing Soledad
wash an excellent gravel road goes to
Palmdale. Not advisable to attempt
to reach Mojave for two or three days
on account of heavy mud just south
of Willow Springs.

Los Angeles to Needles—Road con-
ditiong are rapidly improving over the
National Old Trails, and within the
course of a few days heavy travel will
be resumed over tinen
route.

Los Angeles to Riverside—A few
miles can be saved on this route to-
day. Follow Valley boulevard through

to Ontario,

thence through Puente to Pomona.
From Pomona follow Holt avenue east
and arriving in Ontario
turn left on Euclid avenue after cross-
ing the street car lines and continue
north to Upland on the east side of
the car line. Turn right on the Foot-

boulevard and continue past Cuca-
monga to Rialto, turning right at Rial-
to go south through town and con-
tinue to the Colton avenue road. Turn
left and follow into Colton, turning
right in the center of town at the Au-

Riverside.
TO SAN DIEGO.

Inland route to San Diego—It is
hoped that highway communication
with San Diego over the inland road
can be resumed within two days, but
this depends upon the success of se-
curing permission to plank a railroad
bridge at Elsinore junction. This
structure is weakened at its central

seven weeks before the coast road to
San Diego will be open for its entire
length.
San Francisco coast route—Will be
passable to Santa Barbara within the
course of a few days via Calabasas,
Newbury Park, Conejo grade, El Rio
and Ventura, although quite rough in
numerous places along the ten miles
of unpaved road which will be found
just west of Camarillo and east of
Ventura. Good from Ventura to Santa
Barbara. North of this point it is ad-

| visable for motorists to get detailed in-

formation from Representative Coane
at the Chamber of Commerce in San-
ta Barbara.

To Corona—Road was opened yes-
terday by way of Riverside, Magnolia
drive and Arlington. Numerous de-
tours near Corona.

San Bernardino to Redlands—lIn the
course of two days the bridge over
the Santa Ana River on Tippecanoe
street will be repaired, and travel will
be resumed over the usual route. At
the present it is still necessary to 60
via Colton and over the Bluff road.

Ocean-to-Ocean highway—It is now
possible to reach Palm Springs via
Rediands Junction, Beaumont and
Banning. Some sand will de en-
countered on the road east of Cabazon,
also at White Water crossing, but this
should cause no great amount of
trouble. It is not advisable to co fur-
ther than Palm Springs, although it is
possible to get as far east as Thermal.

Mountain resorts—Among Southern
California's many mountain resorts,
the Arrowhead Hot Springs route is
one of the few available for use at
the present time. Many motorists are
also finding opportunity to visit the
Mission Inn at Riverside.

The Harbor boulevard to San Pedro
is practically impassable on account of
water on the road. Best route is via
Long Beach and Wilmington, over
Long Beach boulevard.

Redondo to Wilmington—Closed,

NE STEP UPWARD
IN SCHOOL LIFE.

COMMENCEMENT. —

Supt. Francis Warns Eighteen
Hundred Young Graduates that
Day of Accidental Success in Life
has Passed and Each Must Have a
Fized Object,

Emphasing the individual] responsi-
bility of the student and congratulat-
ing the 1800 graduates from the Los
Angeles grammar schools upon their
work, Supt. Francis delivered the prin-
cipal commencement address at the
concluding exercise of the eighth
Srade Classes in the auditorium of the
Manual Arts High School, yesterday
morning.

“Seventy-five per cent. of the men
who have attained success today have
attained it by accident,” said Mr.
Francis. “The time has come when
a man to make a success of himself
must begin early and foliow some one
line of endeavor; he must choose his
life work.“

Mr. Francis also gave the prospec-
tive high school students some valu-
able advice in regard to their high
school life. He told in a few words
the dangers of forming bad habits
and choosing wrong companions. As
an encouragement to the graduates he
said, “Make a mark for yourself. Do
— 2 and be something worth
while.”
A large majority of the 1800 grad-
uates were present with their parents.
At an early period the huge auditor-
lum of the school was taxed to its
capacity. Many students were com-
pelled to stand in the aisles.

One of the features of the lengthy
programme was the masterly delivery
by the pupils of their orations. Her-
bert Sturdy, who spoke on the subject
of “Educational Efficiency,” proved a
polished orator. His subject was well
analyzed and his manner of delivery
good. Miss Barbara Miller spoke on
“California Missions.“ Miss Con-
stance Raynard on “Charity,” and
Clara Little gave an oration on the
Liberty Bell.

was furnished by
combined orchestra of the grammar
schools and the students sang their
school songs.

. Rosemont School, which has just
added an eighth grade, had the small-
est list of graduates of al! the schools.
There were but two students,
Morrell and June Huskins.

FRESH BURDEN
ON TAXPAYERS.

“Progressive” Falsity to Cost
Large Sum to Correct.

Nearly Fifty Thousand Voters
M ust Re-register.

Slick Effort to Disfranchise

Partisans is Balked.

It will cost Los Angeles county
$5000 to undo the desperate attempt
by Johnson political tricksters to dis-
franchise 60,000 voters through pur-
posely false registration advice spread
broadcast over the State by, leaders
of the defunct “ ve” party.
About this number will have to re-
register in order to vote at the Presi-
dential primaries.

Basing their opinion on the 1913
primary law, which was upheld by
the State Supreme Court in a ruling
handed down Monday, experts in elec-
tion matters declare that voters must
designate their party affiliation if they
would support any of the candidates
at the August primaries except those
whose names appear on the ballot as
nonpartisan.

Few if any candidates will be on
the ballot under an independent head-
ing, and the voters who desire to
support a Republican or member of
any party eannot do so unless they
have properly registered. Up to last
night more than 46,000 voters were
designated on the registration records
ae “not stated“ and this total is ex-
pected to be increased before
tion deputies leave the field.

“It will cost around $5000 to remedy
this error,” ad Registrar
yesterday.

Among the candidates to be voted
on in August will be those seeking
the nomination for United States Sen-
ator, Congressmen, Senators and
Assemblymen.

Second only to the rebuke given
Johnsonism at the October election
the ruling of the Supreme Court
knocking out the plane of the legisia-
tive filibusters who overrode the will
of the people at the extra session of
the Legislature is looked upon by Re-
publicans as well as members of all
other parties excepting the “Progres-
sives” as a forerunner of an over-
whelming ey for the referendum.

Assemblyman A. L. Bartlett said
yesterday the Feterendum petitions
are now being“ printed and will be
ready for distribution by the end of

the week. He says a State organiza-;|

tion has been effected and every
county will be canvassed for signers.
Los Angeles county has made the best
showing in registrations, more than
150,000 voters having affixed their
names to the Great Register since
January 3, and it le believed that if
it were necessary sufficient signatures
could be secured here to hold up the
amended registration law.

Fighting Dry Plans.

It was learned here yesterday that
strenuous steps are being taken
throughout the country to defeat the
bill now before Congress that would
make the District of Columbia “dry.”

d Appeals were sent to many influential

business men of Los Angeles to send
messages at once to Congressmen and
Senators asking them to vote against

the measure.

One of the received here
said: “If the bill should pass the
American government will be the
laughing stock of the world. The idea
of a measure that would prevent a
foreign diplomat from partak of
his wine or other drinks at his
meals!“

It is generally conceded that the

of the bill would have a de-
termining effect upon the liquor issue
throughout the United States.

ATION” AND HYPOORISY.

No self-respecting nation can 80 to
war without pretentiously claiming

to fight for civilization. The greater the

country, the more superior the brand of
civilization are they fighting for. Huh!

man lecturers in England drew large intel-
lectual audiences, and no English library
was complete without the works of German
men of note. But now the Germans are all
barbarians. They must be utterly annthi-
lated that English civilization may be re-
stored to an aching world. With amazing,
unthinkable callousness some of the great-
est of English statesmen demand the most
hideous fate for Germany. The safest joke
to raise a derisive laugh in England always
contains a contemptuous allusion to Kul-
en good could ever come out of Naza-

It is England at her old game of splendid

. She has never done anything

yet that was not her great moral and relli-
gious duty. Dugland prides herself on her
scruples; she must always find some great
moral issue upon which to fight for what
she wants. Perhaps Bernard Shaw’s sum-

ming up of the English national character

in his “Man of Destiny” best describes the
British brand of civilization. Shaw makes

him master of the world. When he
wants a thing ... he waits pa-
tiently until there comes into his mind
a burning conviction that it is his moral
and religious duty to conquer those who
have got the thing he wants. Then he
becomes irresistible. Like the aristo-
crat he does what he pleases and grabs
what he wants; like the shop-keeper he
pursues his rpose with an industry
and stead ess that come from a
deep sense of moral responsibility. He
is never at a loss for an effective moral
attitude. As the great champion of
freedom and national independence he
conquers and annexes half the world
and calls it colonization. When he
wants a new market for his adulterated
Manchester goods he sends out a mis-
sionary to teach the natives the gospel
of peace. The native kills the mission-
ary and he files to arms in defense of
Christianity, fights for it, conquers for
it, and takes the market as a reward
from heaven. In defense of his island
shores he puts a chaplain on board his
ship, nails d flag with a cross on it to
his top-gallant mast, and sails to the ends
of the earth, sinking, burning and de-
stroying all who dispute the empire of
the seas with him. He boasts that a
slave is free the-moment his foot
touches British soil and selis the chil-
dren of his poor to work under the lash
in factories for sixteen hours a day.
He makes two revolutions and then de-
clares War on one in the name of law
and order. There is nothing so bad or
so good that you will not find English-
men doing it, but you will never find
an Englishman in the wrong. He does
everything on principle,. robs you on
business principles, enslaves you on im-
perial principles, supports his king on
loyal principles, and cuts off his king’s
head on republican principles. His
watchword is always duty, he never

interests is lost.“

True, the English do not now work
children in factories; but that has only
been abolished during the last five minutes
or so, and that indictment was certainly
true in Napoleon’s day when England was
saving civilization from that conqueror as
she ig today from Wilhelm of Germany.

it is only in the last decade that she
has, for Persia's own good, divided Persia
into Russian and British spheres of infiu-

ence; fought a bloody war for the Trans-

vaal gold and diamond mines in South Af-
rica, sent an “expeditionary” force into
Thibet, always in the cause of freedom and

And even now, while half the columns of
her newspapers shriek with the reported
proclamations and speeches of her king and
government anent the importance of anni-
hilating German barbarism, the rest of the
space is taken up with Infinitely keen dis-
cussions on the best way to capture Ger

man trade and insure profitable commercial |

reward for the great sacrifice they are mak-
ing in the cause of civilization.

To the onlooking neutral civilization 18
much the same the world over. In some it
breaks out in frank frightfulness,“ in oth-
ers in smug hypocrisy. It is largely a ques-
tion of whether one prefers being robbed
by a polite highwayman with a silvery
tongue) who does it for your own good, or
by a desperate and hungry man who does
it for his personal advantage.

declares that no confuston exists in

the primary election law and fully shows
the falsity of the claim of the Governor and
Speaker Young that neither party nomina-
tions nor partisan primaries are possible
under the existing law.

Stripped of the political cloak of as-
sumed “public welfare” the Governor and
his associates stand in the stocks exposed

special session of the Legislature the Gov-
ernor asserted that his sole purpose was
to carry out the expressed will of the peo-
ple; and under this guise he foisted on the
State a nonpartisan registration law which

is the very antithesis of the people's will,

and is so construed by the Supreme Court.
“The court is unanimous in the view

| that under the law as it now stands,” said

Chief Justice Angelotti in his oral decision,
“a voter is entitled to have his party affill-
ation stated in his affidavit of registration
and on the Great Register. We think that
the intent is absolutely clear and definite
in this case and could not be clearer.” In
that language there is nothing equivocal;
it sustains fully the attitude of the legal
committee that it was not necessary to
referendum the amended registration law,

Yor the reason that partisan registration

was fully provided for in the main primary
election act. Attorney Thomas V. Cator,
who argued the case before the Supreme
Court, was a consulting member of that
committee. He gave an opinion tmmedi-
ately after the October referendum election
that there was no confusion in the primary
law and that a special session of the Leg
islature would be wholly unnecessary.

Gov. Johnson replied to that interview
with a statement that such a construction
of the law was promulgated, “either through
gross ignorance or malicious mendacity.”
Yet every contention of Attorney Cator was
sustained by the Supreme Court; when he
started to elaborate on gome of his points
the Chief Justice interrupted him, saying
that his points were “too fundamental to
permit argument.” The weapon of vituper-

ation with which the Governor attempted |

to strike down Attorney Cator proves a
boomerang which floors the Governor with
the force of his own sarcasm. It is now for
the apologists of the administration to de
cide whether it was tgnorance of the law
or mendacity that provoked such a retort
from Gov. Johnson.

By its decision the Supreme Court sus-
tains the contentions of the Referendum
Committee that the recent session of the
Legislature was called, not for the purpose
of carrying out the will of the people, but
expressly to defeat that will. The State

was put to the expense of about $20,000 to

enable the Legislature to reenact a law
the main parts of which had been defeated
once by referendum under the 1913 law;
the right was given the elector to state his
party affiliation when registering or to de
cline to do so, providing that he must state
his party affiliation thirty days d More the
primary in order to take part in a party
primary. This law was sustained by the
electorate of the State in the referendum
election last fall; but it was repealed a
second time at the recent special session
of the Legislature. As there is no restric-
tion in the referendum section of the State
Constitution to prevent the re-enactment of
a law once defeated by the referendum, it
will be necessary to circulate referendum
petitions a second time in order to preserve
the partisan features of our State election
laws.

the petitions and place them in circulation, |

justice still survive. The answer to this

E CAN WIN.

With untiring and intelligent and en-
thusiastic effort the Republican party may
be fairly certain of securing a majority in
the Flectoral College next winter, of carry-
ind a majority of the lower house of Con-
gress and of wresting nine Senatorial seats
from the Democrats and filling them with
stalwart Republicans,

Of the ninety-six Senators who represent

the forty-eight States fifty-six are Demo-
crats and forty are Republicans. There are
thirty-two Stdtes in which a United States

Senator is to be elected. Five of these
States are hopelessly Democratic and five

are doubtful. Of the remaining twenty-two
fifteen are strongly Republican and the oth-
er seven are normally so, although in them
the Democrats succeeded in the last elec-
tion in securing Senators whose places will
be filled by Republicans next winter.

Expectations of Republican success next

November are founded upon a solid basis.

“As goes New York so goes the Union.” In

New York the Republican party since 1912 | posing room the next day you could hear

has won back the Governor, the Legislature
and a maſority of the Congressional dele-
gation. There are twentv-four States that
have a Republican majority in their Con-
gress delegation against twenty-one States
with a Democratic majority of Congress-
men, and three States—Nebraska, Utah and
West Virginia—that are evenly divided in
that respect.

Only the war breaking out in July, 1914,
saved the Democrats from an overwhelm-
ing defeat on the tariff issue in November,
1914, and as it was thelr majority in the
lower house of Congress was reduced from
163 to thirty-four.

The. registration in this county shows
that the rank and file of the Progressives
are returning almost en masse to their
proper place in the Grand Old Party, and
the Old Guard welcomes them with open
arms. All that is needed is to sound the
slogan, “In essentials harmony, in non-
essentials liberty, and in all things unity,”
and work for success.

Now, then, “together, brethren!”

A GROUND-HOG CASE.
BY EUGENE BROWN.

celebrated Weather Bureau.

Arctys Monax is the dressed-up Sunday
name of the otherwise unassuming and pa-
tient little ground hog—also passing as the
coy and cosy woodchuck in several sections
of our flourishing land. ,
There were many thriving representatives
of the Monax family here before Columbus
came. In fact, in the days when Eric the
Red sighted the bleak New England coast—
over nine hundred years ago—it was one of
the young Monaxes who first espied that
whiskered Norse adventurer as he clam-
bered over the rail of his scow. He has
watched the growth and settlement of the
country and has quietly retreated before the
advancement of men with blunderbusses,
muskets, repeating rifles and cameras. He
likes to be near, but not of our vaunted
civilization. In pioneer days he furnished
a luncheon for Daniel Boone and he has
been the theme of several of our most an-
cient and respected jests.
In the days prior to the establishment of
our illustrious but abused Weather Bureau
the ground hog was an established authority
on climate. The goosebone took charge of
the weather up to February, but on candle-
mas day the firm paw of the woodchuck
was op the wheel. He was the veiled
prophet of Mercury. All bets on the weath-
er were settled by the ground hog. Back
East we used to buy our garments on the
judgment of this hairy little seer. If he
said we were going to have a long-drawu
winter we promptly laid in a fresh supply
of flannel underwear. If he sighted an open
ig we began to paw over the straw

The methods of the ground hog were
ridiculously simple. All he wanted was a
squint at the sun—or the place f ought
to be. By nature he was so timorous that
the sight of his naked shadow affrighted
him. He and his wife would retire to their
little home in the fall and, after boarding
up the windows and setting the alarm clock
kor candlemas, they would take a prolonged
nap. With nothing to do but sleep and
raise whiskers the time passed very peace-
fully. But on candlemas morn Mrs. Monax
would rout the colonel out and start him

he took down the blinds he would blink
through his galways and behave a good
deal as a man does who emerges from a
moving-picture show into the glorious day.

After practicing a few moments of deep
breathing on the front porch he would step
out into the path to his home and look
about him. If the sun shone brightly and
his shadow was visible he would turn back
into his home and exclaim: “Nothing do-
ing, Martha”—Martha being the name of
his hirsute spouse. So after again putting
up the shutters he would craw! back into
his folding bed and take another snooze of
six weeks. He knew that we were going
to have that much cold and iaclement
weather and he was independent
to keep out of it.

It was a ground hog case.

So everybody got into the habit of watch-
ing the processes of the woodchuck on his
calling day. Even if the day were balmy
and bright and fair we knew that there was
still a month and a half of sleighing ahead
of us. We believed it ‘cause the ground
hog told us so.

The name of the woodchuck or ground
hog does not often appear on the printed
bill of fare, yet the little animal makes a
piquant and savory addition to the larder.
Eating ground hog beats starving to death
all to nothing. The meat would make mag-
nificent goulash. The woodchuck is nor

|} mally fat and tender and, as his fodder is

unobjectionable, he should make cleanly
eating for white men. The origina] ground
hog story recognizes this fact as it deals
with the boy that was digging out the
ground hog—he had to have him ‘cause the
preacher was coming to dinwer.—It was a
ground-hog case.

In the newspaper office which I long in-
fested we had a printer who religiously
celebrated ground-hog day by getting stewed
to the roof. As a matter of fact he got
tanked to the limit most every day, but on
candlemas he had a good excuse. It was

On one occasion he gathered a few bibu-
lous companions about him and the frolic-
some herd came under my window and
warbled that grand old college hymn:
“How much wood would a woodchuck chuck,
If a woodchuck would chuck wood?”

After the singing of nine thousand verses
of this popular air I came out and inquired
what the big doings were all about.

“Zish ish candlemas,“ gargled my satel-

than that. It’s rotten. :

“I sald candlemas,” exclaimed the print
er, thickly. |

“No use trying to hold a candle to you,”
I snorted. “You're lit up already.”

When he came up the gtairs to the com-

him sosh and splash like a jar of butter-
milk. But he was content. He had ob-
served woodchuck day.

It was a ground-hog case.

RIPPLING RHYMES.

EPIDEMIC.

Life is a sad and painful trip for people
who are aging. An epidemic of the grip
o’er all the land is raging. The young men
sneeze a while and laugh, and cough a while
and snicker; the old men break themselves
in half when coughing, and grow sicker.
The young recover when they take of medi-
cine a spoonful, the old men dope and still
they ache, and life is grim and pruneful.
The young lay off a half a day when grip
has sprung its warning, and they are back,
serene and gay, to work tomorrow morning.
The old must sit around the stove for
weeks—which isn’t funny—until] the doc, a
downy cove, has taken all their money. The
old must sit and soak their feet and swal.
low pills and powders, and mustard plas-
ters wear, and eat denatured soups and
chowders. I hate to hear a young man brag
about the way he suffers; he has no richt
to chew the rag among us apcient duffers!

Four-Day Celebration.

Unique in the annals of birthday
celebrations was that of Mrs. Mary A.
Abbott, a resident of the Hotel Vir-
ginia, Long Beach, who celebrated her
eightieth anniversary with a party of
four days” duration, extending from
Friday to Monday.

Un Friday afternoon Mrs. Caroline
Downing was hostess at a birthday
Party ip the Louis XV ballroom. This
was in the nature of a surprise for
Mrs. Abbott, for the table was hid-
den behind screens when she was
cailed in for the reception. After
Mrs. Abbott had received them all the
screeus were suddenly whisked aside
and the tables, were revealed. They
were prettily decorated with candles
and flowers, and on the center one
Was a gigantic birthday cake with a
huge figure 80“ in the center. Six-
teen candles surrounded this. There
were two other tables, one laden with
gifts and the other overflowing with
flowers from Mrs. Abbott’s numerous
friends.

On Saturday evening Mrs. Abbott
was hostess at one of the most elab-
orate and beautiful events ever given
at the Hotel Virginia, the guests in-
| cluding only those who were old
friends. The dinner guests numbered
twenty-two.

The grill on the second floor was
chosen for the affair. Mrs. Abbott,
who fails to look like an octogenarian,
was dainty in a white embroldered
silk crepe, with an exquisite white
polnt lace scarf over her shoulders.

After the first course dinnergrams
were sent to Mrs. Abbote and a num-
ber of the guests. After the second
| Course others were favored with in-
teresting special] delivery letters which
were read aloud, and after the third
course original poems were read.

Kimball Young of Chicago was
| toastmaster, and were made
dy Col. Charles R. Drake, William P.
Nestle, John R. Dr. W. Harri
man Jones and Down-
ing, ending with a toast by Col. Drake
— To the Absent Ones —in reference
to three expected guests who had been
unable to arrive on account of the
roads being washed out, and also to
friends who had passed beyond. Mrs.
Abbott responded, saying that she had
lived eighty wonderful years. and that
she was really sorry for the younger
people of this generation who did not
have the rich store of memories she

Those who enjoyed her, hospitality
at the dinner party were Col. Charles
R. Drake, Mr. Kimball Young, Mr.
and Mrs. D. E. Adams, Mr. and Mrs.
Hubbard Reid, Mr. and Mrs. Timothy
Foley, Mr. and Mrs. W. N. Byers, Mr.
and Mrs. J. E. Tucker, Mr. and Mrs.
A. Pickens, Mrs. Caroline Downing,
Mrs. Frank Roberts, Mrs. J. P. Quirk,
Miss Charlotte Thomas, Miss Ellen S.
Young, Dr. W. Harriman Jones, Mr.
William P Nestle. 7

After the dinner the party joined in
the week-end dance in the ballroom,
and Mrs. Abbott completed her cele-
bration by dancing the one-step with
Dr. Jones as her partner.

On Sunday and Monday Mrs. Ab-
bott wound up her natal day festiv-
ities by receiving and serving in her
apartments.

The Amateur Players are to be con-
Fratulated upon their clever and
finished presentation of Sutro’s The
Two Virtues,” at the Gamut Club last
evening. It was essentially a dramatic
event as well as brilliant socially.

It is high time that we recognize
that these amateur players are a long
way above the average and the plays
they present from time to time are
really worth-while performances,
technically as good as many a travel-
ling professional company, and staged
with considerably more care than is
usually vouchsafed the professional
one-night stand.

Mrs. Henry Van Dyke, an artist of
considerable merit, was entirely re-
sponsible for the scenery at last
night’s performance; actually built as
well as painied it from her own
signs. They received a long round of
applause entirely on their own merits,
those two charming scenes, a rich
masculine library and a dainty
feminine sitting-room. They alone
were sufficient to inspire the actors
to show their best talents.

And the acting was way above what
is expected of the society amateur.
They had thirty rehearsals all told,
and everything went with profes-
sional celerity. The amateur orches-
tra could earn its living In any city.

In these days of moving pictures
and cheap musical comedy, we must
evidently look to our amateurs to
present the “legitimate” to a large
extent. “The Two Virtues” is a de-
lightfully subtle comedy, bristling
with epigrams and naughty jimes at
society.

The principal male role, that of
a comfortable naive bachelor. with
an artiess penchant for polite persi-
flage, was taken by Clarence Hoblit-
zelle of Pasadena, who carried the
part with happy conviction, Mrs.
Conway Evans, in the role of his
deliciously bourgeoise titled’ sister
Lady Milligan, simply rippled with
cultured unpleasantness. Her gowns,
too, called forth special commenda-
tion—loaned, it was whispered, from
Mrs. William May Garland’s imported
wardrobe

Mrs. Raymond Stevens was respon-
sible for the role of the poet’s ir-
repressibly sentimental wife, Mrs.
Jervoise, for whom the bachelor is
understood to cherish a sublimely for-
lorn, igned devotion, which age-
quately protects him from all futtre
pursuit. It is upon this carefully
cultivated devotion that the comedy
hangs, and Mrs. Stevens lost none
of the possibilities of the part. All
the same, Sutro will have the suf-
fragettes on his track if he persists
in depicting such y fool
women.

lady “hopelessly outside the pale,”

Combining a pleasing love theme
with thrills and a touch of mystery,
“My Lady Incog,” starring the beau-
tiful actress, Hazel Dawn, is holding
interest well at Woodley’s theater this
week. Miss Dawn has the role of
Nell Carroll. a southern society girl!
who, upon the death of her guardian, |
finds herself penniless and her home
heavily mortgaged.

Forced to seek employment to save
her home, she accepts employment,
upon the advice of her attorney, with
an agency that has taken up the trail |
of a very baffling robbery in an exclu-
sive summer colony. Miss Dawn en-
ters the role of the girl, who is inter-
ested in the solving of the mystery,
with dash. and plays it with marked
versatility. The cast seen in her sup-
port is satisfying and the settings are
attractive.

THE OLD GUARD.

Frankly, we are of the opinion that
the San Francisco and Salt Lake of
1916 would have caused a riot in the
Coast League once upon a time.

Boxing fans of mature years are
subject to the same illusions, the same
fealty to old idols. None of them wil
hesitate to tell you that Peter Jackson
would have knocked off Jack John-
son's bloomin’ block, and that John I.
Sullivan could have knocked the socks

way to prove that he

wrong.

that said “white hopes classed with
the men who fought when bearhood
was in flower. Furthermore, we re-

day class with the gladiators of twenty
years ago.

Redlands.
REAT GOOD DONE
Y DEEP SOAKING.
WATER IN GROUND WILL LAST
YEARS, SAYS EXPERT.

REDLANDS, Jan. 29.—That the
material value from the heavy rains
of the last fifteen days of the month
will greatly exceed the material dam-
age done in this section by the flood
waters, is the statement of Dr. George
Robertson, biologist of the University
of Redlande.

“The rains have put the ground in
an ideal condition for crops, to be
desired, although some loss is neces-
sary through the washing of the flood
waters,” said Dr. Robertson.

His contention is that the Soll, be-
cause of the heavy rains during the
winter, will be thoroughly soaked,
that many underground lakes will be
formed and that cro for the néx?
three or four years will be made heavy
by the water which has gone into

| the ground, as if it were a sponge. Dr.

Robertson says enough water has al-
ready been stored up to last through
three comparatively dry seasons.

Sees Damaged Bridges.
[LOCAL CORRESPONDENCE. }
COVINA, Feb. 1.—Supervisor Wood-
ley looked at various ruined bridges
in the east end of the San Gabriel
Valley today and met about 300
ranchmen, who were anxious for im-
mediate steps to avert further pos-
sible damage from high water. Mr.
Woodley visited many points where
the orchards had been flooded and dis-
cussed best immediate steps with the
owners. He found the ranch people
generally in favor of drastic elimina-
tion of bridges. It is declared these
have proved a first cause in antagoniz-
ing the flow of streams, causing them
to seek new channels and therefore
do damage.

HAMMO CASE GOES
T0 JURY TODAY.

MERELY PERFORMING DUTY, IS
PLEA FOR PATROLMAN.

Samuel Shammo, police officer on
trial for the killing of Chester Nolen,
a 17-year-old boy, last October, took
the stand yesterday afternoon in his
own defense. He described vividly the
occasion and endeavored to convey the
impression that he and his superior
officer, Sergt. William Cahill, knew the

when they ordered him to halt.

ust prior to his testimony, George
Wesson, a probation officer; Willis
Church, and several other persons
were put on the stand in order to
show that Nolen had a bad record.
Deputy District Attorneys Shelley and
Keyes put every possible weight to
bear on the fact that officers did not
recognize the boys as criminals and
were merely suspicious of their efforts.

For four hours the attorneys in the

argued before the jury.

4 the defense insisted that the of-
ficers were merely performing their
duty in their pursuit and attempted
capture of the fugitives. They insisted
that if persons are allowed to run
away after the officer has called to
halt, all and order would quickly
be eradicated. The numerous killings
of officers recently by criminals were
given very heavy stress.

In marshaling their the
attorneys for the prosecution called
attention to the contradictory testi-
mony of the officers, particularly as
to their knowledge of the victims of
their guns. They insisted that even
though the boys were criminals of
most vicious type, they were both so
young that the police could have ap-
prehended them and held them with-
out use of firearms.

The argument occupied so long a
time that Judge Craig continued the
case until this morning, at which time
he will instruct the jury. No decision
has been made as yet by the office of
the District Attorney as to the pros-
ecution of Sergt. Cahill if Officer
Shammo is acquitted.

Denatured.
NOT LIKE DAYS OF OLD.

Chinatown’s New Tears Celebration
Tomorrow and Thursday Will be
Only a Tame Reminder of
Times of Queues and a
Monarch at Home.

If you hear a din that sounds like
far off cannonading and see the play of
pyrotechnics over the little oriental

village to the east of the Plaza any
time during the next two days, don’t
be alarmed. It will not be the long-
threatened conflict between the Chi-
nese and Japanese, but merely a cele-
bration of the Chinese new year.

There will not be as much noise as
in former years and there will not be
as much mumination, because the
Chinese have changed their method
of celebration. Before China became
a republic Chinese everywhere looked
forward to their annual fiesta as the
most pleasurable event of the year.
Now those in America celebrate the
New Year with Americana.

“We will shoot some fire crackers
and other harmless explosives tomor-
row and Thursday, and will illuminate
our streets.“ said one of the Amer-
icanized members of the colony, last
night, “but it will not be the same
sort of jellification that one time
marked our celebration. It will mere-
I De as a reminder of the time when
we were under monarchical rule. You

know we are a republic gow.”

ters. The case will be continued to-
day.
