REE-LUNCH REPORT
SAYS YES AND NO.

CITY PROSECUTOR PASSES THE
BUCK TO COMMISSION,

—ůůñůñ

Police Board will Take Another
Week ‘to Decide Whether Hot
Beans are Illegal and Cold Beans
are Perm'sible in Saloons of the
City.

City Prosecutor Williams passed
the buck back to the Police Commis-
sion yesterday in thé matter of reg-
ulating the free lunch business in an
opinion which says the commission
can or cannot regulate the menus or

abolish free lunches in saloons—ac-
cording to the point of view or the
interpretation of the opinion.
The first paragraph of the opinion
based on the premise that the
opinion covers only the authority of
the commission to prohibit the “sell-
ing and serving of food for profit“ in
saloons. Continuing, the opinion says:

“Your body unquestionably has the
legal right to control the conduct of
this class of business, and if in your
opinion the serving of food does not
comport with the lawful conduct of
the business, you can regulate or pro-
hibit the serving of same in saloons.

“Your attention is further called to
section 21 of Ordinance No. 20,640
(the liquor ordinance,) which pro-
hibits ‘the carrying on in conjunc-
tion with, or in the same room with,
any saloon any other kind of business.’
Therefore, the serving of food for
profit in connection with a retail liq-
uor establishment is prohibited by this
section ot the ordinance.”’

The request of the hundreds of
restaurant men who petitioned the
Police Commission in the matter is
that the commission issue an order
that free luncn menus be restricted to
crackers and cheese and a little snack
of cold stuff. This leaves the com-
mission to decide that hot beans are
illegal and cold beans come within
the law, while the commission must
also face the fact that by initiative
ordinance the city has voted in favor
of free lunches. It is likely, however,
that the commission wil) issue orders
affecting the two or three saloons that

cash

business about the ranch. The letter

declared that Mason had offered $4000
for the property and that he
was considering this seriously.

Early yesterday morning Mason ap-
proached Kent about their business
deal. Kent said he would sell, and
when the said this Mason refused
pointblank to buy. Words followed,
and Mr. Kent finally declared that he
had no further accommodations for
Mason.

“All right,” Mason snarled. “You
go down to the barn and fix my horse
and get my shoes there and I'll pack
up and get out.”

Mr. Kent, glad to be thus easily
rid of his unwelcome guest, and little
hoping for any board money, went to
the barn, got the stranger's horse
ready, and started back to the ranch-
house with the shoes. As he opened
the back door of the house, Mason
appeared on the threshold, carrying
Kent’« shotgun in his hands

FIRES POINTBLANK.

“You and me'll settle our accounts
right now.“ he shouted, and leveling
the gun, fired pointblank at Mr. Kent.
Quick as the gun’s flash, the rancher
turned sideways, the buckshot ripping
across his left breast.

“Hell! Til get you vet.“ Mason
shouted, and started to fire the other
barrel, but the breech jammed. Kent
turned and ran around the house, to-
wards the Curtis ranch. Mason, still
fiddling with the breech of the gun,
started running after the wounded
man.

The pursver saw his quarry would
reach aid, and turned and disappeared
into the Kent ranch-house, locking
himself in. Mr. Kent collapsed on the
doorstep of his friend’s house. Mr.
Cartis, a young bachelor of 30, rushed
around from the back where he was
working. A series of sharp questions
and answers and Curtis started across
the street, unarmed, to get his friend's
assailant. In the middle of the road
he met Justice Bennett, whose home is
located in a small ravine a short dis-
tance south. e justice had heard
the shooting and was on his way to
find out what it was all about. He
was also unarmed.

Despite their unpreparedness, the
two men ran to the front door of the
Kent ranch-house, and pounding on it,
demanded Mason to open it.

“Keep away or-I'll kill you both!“
Mason screamed at them. Undaunted
Curtis and the justice put their shoul-
ders to the door and smashed it in-
wards. Mason fired, the shot striking
Curtis in the neck, killing him instant-
ly. Justice Bennett seized his falling

even with immediate attention.

Mason was killed and the battle
ended long before Sheriff Cline with
Deputies Reyes, Sepulveda, Fox and
Nolan could arrive on the scene. They
started out in a high-powered
automobile immediately upon receipt
of the news.

SENTENCE STANDS.

The District Court of Appeals has
affirmed the judgment of Superior
Judge Lewis of San Diego county, in
refusing a new trial to E. D. Love,
convicted of lascivious conduct with a
boy, and sentenced to twelve years
in San Quentin.

IN AND OUT.
ABOUT THE COURTS.

DAMAGE SUIT. When the gas
supply was suddenly shut off April
25 last, Will E. Chapman, proprietor
of a poultry ranch in Alhambra,
claims he lost chickens and eggs in
brooders valued at $1027.50. Yesterday
ihe brought suit against the Los An-
geles Gas and Electric Company for
damages in the amount of $2027.50.
Gas was used to obtain artificial heat
for the brooders.

OFFICERS ELECTED. Miss Char-
lotte Caflin of the County Clerk's of.
fice was @lected secretary, and W. T.
Osterholt, vice-president, of the Coun-
ty Emplovees’ Association, at the an-
nual election of officers in the Hall
of Records, Monday night. D. C. Cas-
selman was re-elected president, and
John N. Hunt, treasurer.

was engaged by the New York Motion-
Picture Company June 16, 1915, and
discharged on January 26 last, Lola
May filed suit yesterday to recover

PREFERS CASH. A contract pay-
able on demand before October 1,
1914, signed by D. B. Lyons, and call-
ing for $550, or 3000 shares of stock
of the Cage Engine and Manufactur-
ing Company, is made the basis of a
suit by Kate Hegel against Mr. Lyons
yesterday for the cash, she electing
not to take the stock. It is alleged in
the complaint that Mr. Lyons refused
to pay the money. The contract was
executed July 3, 1914.

A Previous Engagement. |

The Council yesterday declined with
thanks an invitation from the motion
picture censors to meet with that
board and discuss the proposed ordi-
nance eliminating the board, and in
turn the Council directed the censor
board to appear before the Public
Welfare Committee of the Council

City Pensions Proposed.

Pensions for all city employees after
twenty years’ service are proposed in
a petition filed with the Board of Pub-
lic Works yesterday by the Teamsters’
Benevolent Association, and the La-
borers’ Fraternal Protective Associa-
tion. The petition will be referred to
the City Council by the Board of Pub-
lic Works.

ASHINGTON, Dec. 22.—The
House passed the conference
report on the administration
currency bill at 10:46 o'clock tonight
by a vote of 298 to 60 and sent the
report to the Senate, which had
| |}waited in session to receive it before
adjournment for the night.
Prolonged and uproarious cheers
from the Democrats greeted the an-
nouncement of the vote by Speaker
Clark, and many members of the
House hastened over to the Senate
to see the report received there.
Earlier in the evening the Senate had
agreed to vote not later than 2:30
o'clock tomorrow afternoon, and the
leaders regarded it as certain that
the completed bill would be in the
hands of President Wilson for his sig-
nature before tomorrow night.
On the final vote thirty-four
publicans, eleven Progressives and
one independent, Kent of California,
voted with the majority for the re-
port, and two Democrats, Calloway
of Texas and Witherspoon of Missis-
sippi, joined the opposition.
The vote followed a debate of near-
ly three hours, during which the gal-
leries remained crowded with spec-

DECEMBER 28, 10

CURRENCY BILL GOES PRESIDENT WILSON

redeposited in the banks of New York,
Chicago, t. Louis and other desi«-
In times of sudden
financial demands when banks have
loaned up to the full limit of their
resources, these reserves furnish little
relief, because if they are paid out to
meet demands, the banks are left in
a precarious condition.
BASIC PRINCIPLE.

The basic principle of the new law
is to get these reserve funds out into
circylation when necessary without
lessening the safety of any bank, and
to provide a place to which local
banks may rush in a crisis and get
cash for the “prime commercial pa-
per” they hold in their vaults.

This is to be accomplished through
a chain of regional reserve banks or
“reservoirs of reserves,” in which al!
banks shal] deposit a stated part of
the money they are required to hold
as reserves. Under tle new system
when a financial flurry comes, the
banks can take commercial paper,
such as notes, drafts and bills of ex-
change to these “reservoirs,” and se-
cure the use of their own reserves, or
if necessary, even the reserve of other
banks, by depositing this security.

The new regional] banks will receive
about one-half of the bank reserves of
the country. They in turn will be
permitted to loan back to the banks
all but 85 per cent. of these reserves,
so that in case of emergency millions
of cash can be breught out into circu-
lation quickly. The banks will have
to pay for these loans, however, as
individuals have to pay for a loan from
any local bank, and this charge is ex-
pected to prevent the too free use of
the reserves held by the regional
banks.

CALIS SCHMIDT ABNORMAL.

Alienist Declares the Former Priest
Said It Was Nobody's Business if He

Piayed Violin in Bath Tub.

[BY A P. NIGHT WIRE To THE TIMES.)
NEW YORK, Dec. 22.—The pro-
‘cession of alienists began their march
to the witness stand today at the trial
of Hans Schmidt for murder. After
Dr. Smith Ely Jelliffe of New York
had testified for the defense, court ad-
journed to enable Schmidt's attorneys
to construct @ hypothetical question
which will be put to Dr. Jelliffe and
to other medical experts.

Practically all Dr. Jelliffe’s testi-

mony indicated that Schmidt was ab-
normal. The witness said the priest
complained to him that hie bishops
and fellow clergy “refused to acknowl.
edge his authority.” The defendant
excused his forgeries of the signature
— his professor at Munich by say-

“I was in high spirits and good
health and I entered into the 4
sonality of the professor. I was the
professor. So it was not wrong for
me to sign his name.”

Dr. Jelliffe asked Schmidt if he ever
played the violin in a bath tub, as one
of the witnesses testified. “I did,”
sald Schmidt. “It was nobody's bus-
mess. I felt like it and I put my feet
in the water and sat in it and played.
What an inspired man does, heaven
wishes him to do.”

During one of his visits to Schmidt's
cell, said Dr. Jelliffe. another physi-
clan who accompanied him pricked
his forefinger with a needie and
showed the prisoner a drop of blood.
Instantly Schmidt's face became livid.

“All blood is mine,“ he shouted,
making a lunge for the physician's
hand, trying to raise it to his lips.

CLEVELAND, Dec. 22.—Boxers
from Ohio, Illinois, Michigan, Wiscon-
sin, Minnesota and Iowa will partici-
pate in the Amateur Athletic Union
boxing tournament which will be held
at the Cleveland Athletic Club here on
the nights of January $ and 16.
Six classes will be contested at 108,
heavy weights, all above 158 pounds.

FROM HIS MOTHER’s TOWN.
AN ADDRESS TO WILSON.

(BY A. P. NIGHT WIRE TO THE TIMES.)

WASHINGTON, Dec. 22.—ir Ce-
eil Spring-Rice, the British Ambassa-
dor, called on President Wilson t-
day for the firet time since last
spring. The Ambassador has only
recently recovered from a long M-
ness. He presented a copy of an em-
boased address to the President from
the people of Chélsea, Eng. In
that town the mother of the Presi-
dent was born and there ffom 182¢
to 1835 the President's grandfather,
the Rev. Thomas Woodrow, was pas-

; tor of the Congregationalist Church.

Federal Job for Colorado Man.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 22.—(By A.
P. Day Wire Henry Clay Hall, for-
mer Mayor of Colorado Springs,
Colo, and once president of the Colo-
rado State Bar Association, was con-
sidered for one of the vacancies on
the Interstate Commerce Commis-
sion at a conference today between
President Wilson and Senator
Thomas and Representative Seidom-
ridge. It is believed to be settled
that President Wilson will reappoint
Commissioner Judson C. Clements of
Georgia.

Bartholt to Retire.

WASHINGTON, Dec: 22.—IBy A.
P. Day Wire.] Representative Rich-
ard Bartholdt of St. Louis, Who has
represented the Tenth Missouri Dis-
tfict in the House for twenty-two
years, has issued a statement saying
he will not be a candidate for re-
election when his term expires in
1915. He expects to work for uni-
versal peace.

Barteson for Civil Service.

WASHINGTON, Dee. A.
F., Day Wire. Post master-General
Burleson has taken a stand againet
the proposal to take assistant post-
masters from the protection of the
civil service, which te embodied in

‘ithe annual appropriation bill now in

the hands of the House Postoffice
Com mittee.

Another Lobby Mant.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 22.—fRy A.
F. Day Wire] Investigation to dis-
close whether a lobby exists to in-
fluence appropriations and legisila-
tion for the District of Columbia and
business corporations of that city was
proposed in a resolution today by
Representative Prouty of Iowa.

GENTLEMAN THREW A BRICK.

Pug Becomes Enraged at Woman
Who HRepulised His Advances and
Muris Bit of Paving.

VENICE, Dec. 22.—Resorting to
the custom of courting of the stone
age is not countenanced by the Ven-
ice police. They arrested this after-
noon “Micky” Sullivan, well-known
lightweight boxer, who is accused of
throwing a rock at Tiny Broadwick,
the girl aeronaut, because she would
not become his bride. Miss Broad-
wick took exceptions to the advances
of Sullivan, who worked at the Race
for life concession between boxing
matches. “Micky” made a final ap-
peal this afternoon, say the police,
and, being again repulsed, is said to
have shied a cobble at Miss Broad-
wick. Hence the battery charge,
which will be heard before Justice
Rennie tomorrow.

Porterville,
NS FOR TWO

CAUSES SOME CHANGES,

Odd Fellows Will Build a Three-
Story Structure Which Will Be
Largely Devoted to Office Purposes.
Another Investor Decides to Dou-
ble the Size of Proposed Building.

PORTERVILLE, Dec. 22.— 80
great has been the demand for busi-
ness locations and 80 brisk have been
the deals in leases on business prop-
erty now under construction that
within the past two days radical
changes to enlarge quarters have
been made in the plans for two new
blocks.

Members of the LO. O. y. lodge, who
recently approved plans for a two-
story temple to be erected in the
Main-street business district at Cleve-
land, commissioned the architect to
increase the size of the building to
three stories. The lodge will occupy
the third story; offices will be pro-
vided on the second floor and the
lower floor will
cantile location.
Build Committee of the lodge
ht that all the leases
already en signed up., al-
theugh work hag only been com-
pleted on the foundation of the block.

V. D. Knupp, a pioneer business
man and property owner, who re-
cently approved the plans of a San
Francisco architect for a two-story
building on Main street, near Put-
nam, has changed his instructions
with regard to the building and will
add materially to the cost to practi-
eally double the size of the struc-

ture.

In the Knupp block there are three
fine store locations, provided on the
lower floor, and Mr. Knupp has stat-
ed that leases are already executed
for all three of them.

& Rodgers, whose new
lock, on Main, near Cleveland, is
well under way. have also teased

their entire building, including sec-
ond floor apartments and offices, and
store locations on the ground floor.

FREE MAIL DELIVERY.
LINDSAY, Dec. 22.—C. E. Brog-
don, the postal inspector for the dis-
trict which includes Lindsay, was a
visitor here yesterday, and at the
conclusion of a conference with the
postmaster, he stated that he will
Immediately make out a recommen-
Gation for the inception in this city
of free delivery of mall.
There are some conditions, with re-
gard to the proper numbering of
houses and the naming of the streets
whieh must be attended to before the
gervice can be started, but the mem-
bers of the City Council have prom-
ised to have all these conditions niet
immediately.
Brogdon stated that in all proba-
bility the new service could be start-
ed within the next ninety days.

CANNED OLAVES.

TULARE, Dec. 22.—Canned olives
are to be an important product of
the Tulare cannery, according to the
plans of Manager Vernon Campbell,
who admitted yesterday that for the
past several weeks he has been gon
tracting for the delivery of Tulare
county fruit, and that he has alread:
several cars of pickling olives in
process.

These olives will be put out un-
der a Tulare county rand, and
Campbell states that as far as the
fruit ie concerned there is nothin:
in California which will equal the
product of the Lindan and Terra
Bella districts, from which his chief
supply has come thus far. At this
time the acreage of olives in the
county is limited, but Campbell hor
the new product will keep pace with
the increased acreage and every ef.
fort will be put forth to market only
the very highest possible grade.

WHEN INTOXICATION PAYS?
Antonio Guerra was convicted of
manslaughter in Judge Willis’s court

yesterday. The evidence showed that
he stabbed H. Maldonado June 7 in a
drunken quarrel on Jackson street.
The evident intoxication of the de-
fendant at the time of the affray was
in his favor, according to Deputy Dis-
trict Attorney Doran, who prosecuted
the case. If the defendant had been
sober and had shown intent, the ver-
dict might have been murder, accord-
ing to the prosecutor.

OBSCENE LETTER CHARGE.

Charies D. Smith of Riverside was
committed to the County Jall in de-
fault of $500 bond by United States
Commissioner Charles N. Whlllame
yesterday on a charge of sending an
obscene letter through the mails to
Miss Lena Darling of that city. Smith
is employed at a hotel in Riverside.

PLEAD NOT GUILTY.

In the United States District Court
yesterday C. 8 McKelvey and W. 1
Btevens, attorneys of this city, indicted
for using the mails in a conspiracy
to blackmail, pleaded not guilty, and
the cases will be set for trial at the
January term of court. A motion
made on behalf of McKelvey for a
severance and separate trial, as the
indictment did not charge a partner-
ship between the defendants, was not
allowed.

DISTRICT COURT ADJOURNS.

With the adjournment of the United
States District Court yesterday noon
there will be no more sessions until
next Monday, allowing all employees
the usual holiday recess. With the
calendar of Monday disposed of, there
will be another adjournment for a
week, covering the New Year holl-

days.

TO HELP UNEMPLOYED.
The Supervisors agreed yesterday
to investigate the exact situation as to
the unemployed in the city and coun-
ty. If the Municipal Charities Com-

mission reports a pressing need that
work be given deserving men, it will
be provided temporarly by the coun-
ty. Workmen are needed in con-
structing several roads.

State courts. However, if the entry-

the alleged claimants had no real in-
terest In the land, and that the entries
were not made in good faith.

that there was a great deposit of salt
in the vicinity of these claims, but
that they have ever been made a suc-
cess commercially the records in the
local Land Office do not indicate.

OUR SCHOOL SYSTEM.

Fiery City Should Work Out Its
Methods According to Needs.
After Exhaustive Travel He Pro-
Poses to Return to Paris and Write
Thesis About Our Doings.

Prof. Henri A. Goy who arrived at
the Angelus yesterday is enjoying the
rare privilege of a world tour without

“around the world” scholarship from
the Paris University and all of his
trave t expenses for one and one-
half years will be paid out of a fund
for that purpose by Albert Kahn, @
noted banker of the French capital.
The travel scholarship is awarded
yearly to one male professor. Each
year the same institution awards «4
scholarship to one woman teacher
which entitles her to a tour through
Europe and America with all expenses
paid.

The rectpients of the scholarships
choose their own special subjects for
investigation and at the conclusion of
their travels write a thesis which is
submitted to the university.

Prof. Goy is making a special study
of echool administration in North and
South America. He wil! give his spe-
tal attention to colonial politics in
Oceanica, Asia and Africa. The visitor
spent yesterday studying the adminis-
tration features of the local public
school system. He talked with Super-
intendent Francis and other local
educators.

“The diversity of methods ts one of
the interesting features of the edu-
cational system in America,” Prof.
Goy said last evening. “For instance,
in Chieago and San Francisco the
boards of education are appointed.
Here in Los Angeles the board ts
elected. The difference in the meth-
ods appears to ba not so much the
result of haphazard procedure as the
desire to let every city work out its
educations system according to its
peculiar needs and environments.
“The general plan followed in this
matter has the advantage of giving
plenty of opportunity for originality.
“| selected the subject of school
administration for the reason that it
appears to me to be one of the most
vital considerations of education. In
the old days when schools were smal-
ler, administration was largely a mat-
ter of the personality of the teacher.
The growth of population and the
consequent increase in the size of the
schools has made administration a
different and more vital question,
“School administration involves
discipline, the regulation of the teach-
ing force and a number of other ques-
tions that reach very close to human
nature. I am obtaining information
in America on my subject that is
very interesting and helpful.”

It has been the custom in France
for the government to reward the
students of the “around the world”
course with important political posi-
tions. One of the traveling scholars
who wrote an especially brilliant
thesis upon his r@turn was recently
appointed Minister of Commerce by
the French government.

Our Rates Highest Among
Twenty Nations,

(BY A. r. NIGHT WIRE To THE TIMEA )

WASHINGTON, Dec. 22.—Govern-
ment ownership of the nation’s tele-
phone lines would cost less than
$900,000,000, and would present no
greater difficulties of financing than
did the Panama Canal, Representa-
tive Lewis of Maryland told the
House today in an exhaustive analy-
sis of his proposal to have those lines
operated by the Postoffice Depart-
ment.

“The perversion of the laws of pubs
Me and private financiering,” said Mr.
Lewis, “by which public governments
have been disinherited of their nor-
mal functions has led to such corrup-
tion and demoralization that cities
like New York with its street rall-
ways, Philadelphia with its gas
works, and San Francisco, with its
telephones, have shamed the scions
of Roman corruption in their most
dishonorable days.“

Although
leson, in his annual report, —
the principle ot government owner-
ship of telegraph and telephone linea,
—— „ has not taken «6
Position on question and not
up — mind.
“Investigation discloses that
telegraphic rates are the highest
among twenty countries,” Mr. Lewis
continued. “The result of these ab-
normal rates is that we rank only
ninth as telegraph users. Against
these conditions it appears that our
postal rates average lower than
ber ef letters hens le

the X *
“The telegraph companies seem

be lacking in institutional economy 8
efficiency. The

ices and
processes, not les than fifty of which
would be replaced by affixing the
postage stamp. The American ine
ciency is further exaggerated by the
duplication of telegraph offices in all
important towns and cities, and the
denial of the service at many thou-

nd necessary poin

A striking feature of the discov-
ery is that the telegraph service is
a relatively declining institution and
that it would be unwise now to
postal it alone and as a single
service. To take over the telegraph
lines alone and operate them mere-
ly as telegraph lines might result in
postal bankrucpty.

But our telephone tolls and
tance rates compare with those of
other countries even less favorably
than do our telegraph rates. It is not
ufifair, or inaccurate tosay that the
American interurban telephone rates
are the scandal of public service
rates the world over. The American
Telephone monopoly takes the thir-
teenth place among seventeen coun-
tries with regard to the lowness of
these rates.

“The local rates of the Bell tele
phone monopoly are just twice the
average charge in other countries,
While our postal rates give us the
first rank in lowness of charges, this
company ranks but fourteenth among
raxteen countries with its ilecal
charges, and we are one of three
countries where the charge for «
lecal call exceeds the letter postal
rates, the other thirteen countries
giving a much lower similar phone
call than their letter rates,

“The subscribers’ rates in Ameri-
can cities, compared with continental
cities, are about three times as high.
For example, in New York, 5400 calls,
about fifteen a day. under measured
service, cost more than the four wn-
itmited yearly vates of London, Paris,
Berlin and Stockholm, together. For
like services, Baltimore pays more
than the rates for London and Parte -
combined, and Washington pays as
much as the five cities of Amsterdam.
Rotterdam, Auckland, Tokio and
Copenhagen combined. In postal tele-
phone countries the local toll tariffs
tend to run about one-half
charge for a letter, while here it runs
with the street car and some-
times exceeds it, when it ts three
times the letter rate.

“While competition does not sup-
ply a remedy because it divides the
service and necessitates the payment
for two phones, yet it throws an
interesting sidelight on the tendency
of a private monopoly to push up
the rates. Thus, of sixty of the
great American cities, twenty-four
averaging 342,486 in population, pay
an average annual phone rate of $53
under competition: while the other
thirty-six cities, averaging only 188.
629 in population, without competi->
tion, pay an average rate of $81.
Since competition can only augment
the total cest of operation, it is ap-
parent how private monopoly and
high rates go hand in hand.

“It will be unnecessary to take
over the telegraph lines here (capt-
talixed at $246,000,000,) as beth
kinds of communication can be han-
died on the telephene wires, which
exceed the telegraph wires in mile-
age and geographical distribution.

“The cost of acquiring the tele-
phone networks is indicated at tome-
thing. lees than 3990,00 for
which [ft is proposed to fesue per
cent. bends. payable In fifty .
Tt is calculated that the ays-
tem. by superimposing the telegrar>
service on the telephone lines at half
present telegraph rates, may net
some fifty millions annually from
that traffic alone, which, with the
present profits of the telephones, and
after the deduction of interest on the
bonds and depreciation. would sup-
ply the department with a large sur-
plus for extensions and so forth.”

IN CHRISTIAN WORK.

G. N. Wrisley, son of George .
Wrisiey, and a student in the Oberlin
Theological Feminary, Oberlin, O., hase
been chosen a member of one of the
three gospel teams sent out Gurt
the Christmas vacation for practi
constructive Christian work among.
young men and boys in the rural com-
munities tn the vicinity of Oberlin.
As soon as classes are suspended for
the recess these deputation teams take
up thetr headquarters in some rural
community and organize en aggres-
sive campaign, general and individual,
to interest boys and young men in the
problems of effective Christian citizen-
ship, working in co-operation with the
local churches. The aim is to stir up
a wholesome interest in the commut-
nity in the practical effielency of
Christian manhood as to the
community life, “

Reclamation Expert Coming.

Edmund T. Perkins, president of
the National Drainage Congress, will
arrive in this city tomorrow from
Chicago, in the interest of the work
of that body. A bill is now pending
before Congress, providing for Fed-
eral supervision of the work of flood
protection and control, and the
drainage of swamp and overflowed
lands. Mr. Perkins was formerly con-

with the United States re-

nected
clamation service.

The Municipal Charities Commis-
—.— Was yesterday busily engaged in
irmishing about the city seek a

suitable location for the

Municipal Labor Bureau. Money for
the purpose was appropriated some
time ago by the City Council and
will become available after January
1. President Johnson said yester-
Gay that he hopes to have a number
of sites to present today for the con-

Sideration of the commission. Dr

Biggest Week in History.
The total postal receipts at the lo-
eal office for the past week amounted

to $82,192.60, the largest in the his-

tory of the city. The figures for Sat-

urday were $12,737.12. The arrivals

of the holiday mail from the East
yesterday were very heavy, but there
Was no delay either in the handling
of the first-class mail or the parcel
pe packages. Postmaster Harrison

more than satisfied with the test
of the utility of the parcel post sys-
tem during the holiday season.
There has been nothing to complain
of either on the part of the officials
of the postoffice or its patrons.

Careless Woodsmen Fined.
Supervisor Chariton of the Los An-
National Forest

geles went to Pasa-
dena yesterday to attend the hearing
of J. B. MeClement and Harry. Gros- |

venor, charged with starting the fire
that resulted about two months ago
in the most disastrous fire in the re-
cent history of the forest service,
burning over five square miles of
territory and costing about $6000.
The men, it appears, were at work
clearing up a piece of woods and
allowed a fire to be unattended and
wnextinguished when they quit work.
Both men were found guilty and fined
$150 each by Justice McDonald.

Mysteriously Hurt

Fred Latshaw, a young man, who
for some time has been in charge
of the govermment’'s Converse Flat
forest nursery, about forty miles back
of Rediands, was taken to the hos-
pital at that place yesterday, suffer-
ing from injuries that are likely to
prove fatal. The boy's skull is said
to be fractured, his face is bruised,
and he has net spoken since he
dragged himself up to the Seven-
Oaks resort, three miles away, from
the nursery on Sunday. No one
knows how he was hurt and forestry
Officers have gone to the nursery with
a view of solving the mystery.

is the wholesale rate fixed by the State

nounced yesterday. This is a reduction
of 4 cents from the contract rate at
which natural gas is now delivered to
the distributing companies in this
city.

ET’S ALL GO
TEACH TANGO!

Dancing-Master Making Twice
as Mach as President
Wilson Gets.
Tango teachers in Los Ange-
les get twice as much for their
work as the President of the
United States, according to
sworn testimony in police
court yesterday in connection
with the arrest of C. M. Meikle-
john, teacher of the new
dances. He was arrested at the
Dagmar Apartments, where, the
officers declare, he was con-

ducting a dancing school.

Investigation by License In-
spector McPhillips showed, he
says, that Meiklejohn was
“earning” $3000 a week by his
teaching. His pupils number
more than 500 and he charges
$3 a lesson. That was the
charge he made to representa-
tives of the license inspector's
office. Each of the pupils re-
ceives two lessons a week,
making de weekly for each of
the 500 people, according to the
officers.

Meiklejohn is fighting the
contention of the police de-
partment that he is conducting
a dancing school. The license
to operate in peace would cost
him $50 for three months, or
what is alleged to be one-six-
tleth of his weekly earnings.

Railroad Commission will be based
the rate to prevail within the city.
The 14-cent rate is the result of an
investigation made by the State Rail-
road Commission after an appeal was
made by the City Council . The com-
mission held public hearings in Los
Angeles, continuing for ever days,
and has just completed the analyzing
and consideration of the evidence ad-
duced at these hearings. The rate will
not be over 56 cents a thousand and
will probably be less.

cedure will be for the Board of Pub-
lie Utilities. This board has received
no official notice of the action of the
State Railroad Commission, but yes-
terday afternoon Commissioners
Wright and Wirsching discussed the
subject and decided to appeal to the
City Attorney for advice as to the
basis of the board's next move, as the

natural and artificial gas is delivered

HE’S OFF WITH OLD >
BEFORE ON WITH NEW.

HE honeymoon of Mr. and Mrs.
T carton B. Parsons of No, 436

South Virgil avenue was inter-
rupted by a mysterious mission to
San Francisco by the groom in which
another woman, private detectives
and attorney and other persons fig-
ure.

Parsons, who is the owner of a
moving-picture theater at Seventh
and Hartford streets, said yesterday
that he went to San Francisco to
“settle a friendship” with Mrs. John
Fisher, the divorced wife of a New
York theatrical man, and that he had
no intention of remaining:away from
his bride.

Attorney Earl Rogers went to San
Francisco and returned to this city
with Parsons Sunday. Private de-
tectives, said to have been employed
by the young man's mother and other
relatives, located him at the St.
Francis Hotel in the northern city.

Parsons and Miss Marian L. Huene,

the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. E. A.
Huene oof the Sharon apartments,

The groom is 28 years old and the
bride 29.

“I simply went to San Francisco to
settle an old friendship with Mrs.
Fisher,” Parsons explained. “We
were very good friends before I was
married and I went north to give «4
proper ending to our friendship and
to explain some things which ed
to be explained. I saw Mrs. er
and was successful in my mission.

“I was in San Francisco only thir-
ty-six hours and that is longer than
I expected to be there. I went to a
dinner and missed the train on which
I had expected to leave for Los An-
geles, or the private detectives never
would have discovered me. My wife
had nothing to do with employing
the detectives. They were put on my
trail by some of my relatives, who
evidently had fears that I might not
return to Los Angeles. Those fears
were unwarranted.”

Mrs. Parsons was at home yester-
Gay with her husband. She refused
to discuss the case. “Cut it out,” was
her only reply to a question.

Mra. Fisher is a handsome blonde,
about fifteen years older than Par-
sons. She came to this city fow
years ago and has lived at several
different fashionable apartment-

As an accompaniment to the salad
course nothing is more tasty than
cheese blocks. To one cupful of soft
crumbs take one cupful of grated
cheese, one egg, one-fourth teaspoon-
ful of salt and a dash of paprika.
Turn out on a board, roll to about
one inch in thickness and cut into
inch squares. Dip in egg and bread
crumbs and fry in deep fat until they
are a rich brown.

The use of chiffon taffeta is be-
coming more general; it forms the
basis of stunning and even-
ing frocks.

The plainer skirts are very short,
cut to the boot tops, exposing con-
trasting uppers; but they are used
only for walking.

There is no good reason for dis-
carding your last season's evening
gowns and wraps. They can be re-
modeled with small expenditure of
time and money.

The young girls are wearing with
simple frocks of ‘velvet or serge gir-
dies of wide silk braid in striped de-
sign. Long tassels of silk are at-
tached to the end.

Fashionable women are wearing
chic little turbans of satin, trimmed
with fur. The material is swathed
about the head in Persian fashion. A
high bow usually trims the side or

front.

Wraps are often worn throughout
the evening at the play. The wonder-
ful fur-trimmed brocades hanging off
the shoulders are a charming back-
ground for the delicately charming
gowns.

You are permitted to wear a
sleeve to the knuckles, if you desire,
in your ball gown, and ff you have a
good arm, you can fasten the upper
points of your bodice over the shoul-
der with a small jewel.

The stout woman should know
that yellow increases her natural
size. Satin also makes her look big-
ger. Blue is a slightly enlarging tone;
white is a stationary color. Black,
geal brown, navy blue and the deepest
of crimsons are all tones that decrease
the size.

A VISITOR.

Improve the River Bed.
LOS ANGELES, Dec. 22.—[To the

Editor of The Times:] A petition to
provide work for the unemployed men
of the city has been presented to the
Council.

I would suggest that one of the best
schemes to adopt would be the im-
provement of the river bed.

If rumors are correct, one or more
new railroads are about to come into
Los Angeles. The city should in
a position to take advantage of ‘this
fact. The natural entrance would be
along the river bed. The improve-
ment could be made a large revenue
producer to the city, and the cost
would be comparatively low.

The city owns its own cement plant,
the river bed would furnish the rock,
sand and gravel necessary, the city
engineering department could supply
the technical forces, and very few
skilled laborers would be required.

With a solid concre enbankment
on both sides of the river bed, and
a cemented epiliway in the center for
the flaedwaters, the city would be
enabled to offer any rallroad a right
of Way upon terms profitable to the
eity and reasonable to the railroad.

It would be a splendid public work,
safeguard our bridges and remove an

THEFT OF SCENARIO CHARGE,

Writer for Universal Film Com-
pany Made Defendant in Suit in Po-
lice Court.
Theft of a scenario submitted to
the Universal Film Company is
charged by Mark E. Jones, who yes-
terday swore to a larceny complaint
against Hampton Del Ruth. The lat-
ter is employed as a writer of scen-
atios by the company, according to
the complaint. He was arrested at
the Photoplayers’ Club last night.
Originally tue complaint was made
against Harrison Del Ruth, who was
killed by Jesse E. Jones at Court street
and Grand ivenue, April 17, last.
Harrison Del Ruth was also a writer
of scenarios, and in obtaining his
data, Mark Jones secured the wrong
name. The error was quickly cor-
rected, but for a Yew minutes the
agents of the City Prosecutor's office
were searching for a dead man that
they might serve a warrant of arrest
on him.
In his complaint Jones recites that
submitted a scenario named

»Hatred's Endless Chain” to the Uni-

versal Film Company for considera-
tion. He wrote it, he says, on paper
bearing his embossed name. Del
Ruth, he claims, struck out the name,
and sent the scenario to an eastern
moving picture company, claiming it
as his own.

The eastern company, Jones says,
had used several of his scenarios and
was familiar with the letterhead. The
company at once wrote him, inquiring
how it came about that Del Ruth
should submit a scenario on Jones's
letterhead, and (he theft was exposed,
he alleges.

It is the firat time that the theft of
a scenario has been brought to crim-
inal action in the Police Court here.

Christmas mail, postoffice officials
were able to devote time toa review ot
the past four days, which has been
the largest in the history of the local
office.

gest day of the holiday rush, 174

BOND CAMPAIGN.

Starting their campaign of educa-
tion the Harbor Bonds Committee has
called a mass meeting at the Forum
tomorrow night on the matter of the
importance of the city voting a $650,-
000 harbor bond tue for the ex-
tension of the jetties and the deepen-
ing of the channels. Talks will be
made by W. H. Bennett, J. A. Romin-
ger, Fred Faulstich, C. H. Windham,
Rev. H. K. Booth and E. F. Van Hoe-

why Pasadenans should be idle when

we have the means to supply them

with work and when ere are im-

provements that should be made.”
CITY BRIEFS.

The women of the Sha

society of the Fraternal Brotherhood
in special meeting elected A. V. Old-
ham as president for the ensuing year.
The Antelope Valley was visited by
the storm which was general through-
out California. In the floor of the
valley the precipitation was recorded
as over one-half of an inch, while in
the vicinity of the foothilis it was
much heavier. The total rainfall to
date is .72 inch as against .69 inch
at this time last year. ;
Under auspicious circumstances, the
Citisens’ League of Antelope Valley
was launched here last Saturday. Sev-
enty-five prominent residents were
present at that time, and a strong
organization was effected. It is the
purpose of this new league to make
a strong fight for the construction of
a county highway through the Ante-
lope Valley, af at present this large
territory has not one inch of first-
class road. No benefit will be derived
from the tate highway, which will
be constructed fifty miles to the west,
and to date none of the bond money

A new use has been found for a
bank book. Mrs. William Dundon,
just arrived in the city, came down-
town today and forgot where she
lived. She appealed to a drug store
and the police were sent for. In-
vestigation showed that she had a
bank account. The local bank was
called up and Mrs. Dundon was given
directions to her lodgings on Linden
avenue.

Army of Unemployed Marching on
Fresno Will Be Received in Ap-
proved Christmas Fashion.
FRESNO, Dec. 22.—Word was re-
ceived at noon. today that 120 mem-
bers of the army of unemployed are
within five miles of the city limits
: and wil) arrive here late this after-
noon. The marchers are badly in
need of both food and clothing and
‘| guffered much because of last night's
and today’s rain. The “invaders”
will be met by the Chief of Police
and Sheriff. who will distribute both
food and clothing. Many city resi-
dents today expressed their willing-
ness to contribute. It ts probable
that the unemployed men will re-
main here a day or two before pro-
ceeding on their march to Bakersfield
and Los Angeles.

Many have deserted after finding
work, but new recruits are being
added daily. |

Pict.
CORONA, Dec. 22.—G, C. Alexan-

der, City Marshal of Corona, was
murdered early today in a shack that
had been occupied by Mexicans. Al-
exander was summoned from his bed
before dawn to quell a supposed dis-
turbance at the shack. The moment
he entered the door a bullet entered
his heart.

It is believed that the marshal was
the victim of a deliberate plot to kill.
Two weeks ago he received anony-
mous letters, warning him that soon
he would be killed.

SOUTH PASADENA, Dec. 22.—In-
stallation of officers of South Pasadena

chapter No. 112, Royal Arch Masons,
took place last evening in Masonic
Hall. There was a goodly attendance
of Royal Arch Masons and their im-
mediate families. The

retary; Hartley C. Packer, Captain of
the Host; William O. B. Foster, Prin-
cipal Sojourner; Eber Wilde,
Arch Captain;

Hoard, Sentinel; John Bdward Sen-
well, Chaplain and Historian.
Following the installation a mus
cal programme was presented by Miss
Hamm, vocal solo; Orval Wesner, pia-
no solo; Ben Lloyd of Los Angeles
sang Harry Lauder’s favorite, “I Love
a Lassie: J. V. Auriemma, baritone
solos, and a piano duet by Mra. R.
S. Payne and daughter, Miss Gladys.
The guests then repaired to the ban-
quet hall, where High Priest R. &.

fine talks were made by the visitors.
CITY’s Loss.

In the death of C. W. Post, South
Pasadena has lost one of its valued
citizens. Although of a retiring nature,
he had made many friends during his
seven years’ residence in this city, and
| for twelve years previous to that time
when he lived in Los Angeles. He
was a native of Pennsylvania, but
came to Los les nineteen years
ago from Indiana.

He was a member of the Godfrey
Post in Pasadena, and with a num
ber of them visited the rg
battlefield last June at the time of
the commemoration of the fiftieth an-
niversary of the battle of Gettysburg.
Mr. Post, who resided at No. 715 Fre-
mont avenue, was a veteran of the
Civil War, and was in many important
engagements. He was a member of
Co. A, Fifty-seventh Pennsylvania
Volunteers, and served three years in
the army of the Potomac, participat-
ing in important engagements in the
battles of Gettysburg, Wilderness, in
which battle he was wounded: Glen-
dale, Malvern Hill, Manassas Junc-
tion, Chancelorsville—in the latter
battle, with a number of others, he
was given the “Kearney Cross,”
named after the general commanding
the corp, in honor of distinguished
service.

His death was sudden, caused from
a stroke of apoplexy, and besides a
widow, he is survived by four sons,
Charles A. Post of Los Angeles, Merit
O. Post, and Elwyn H. Post of Chi-
cago, Rule B. Post of Bend, Or., and
one daughter, Mrs. E. 8. Ware of Fo-

mona.
FOOTBALL STAR.

Sidney Foster, the son of Mr. and
Mrs. William Foster, No. 1126 Bl Cen-
tro street, is one of the few players
who has been selected by all the foot-
ball experts for a place on the All-
Southern California football team.

Foster, who is a sophomore at Oc-
cidental College, has played left-half
on his varsity team for two years and
he has been in every important game.
He is considered one of the headiest
players ever seen in the south, and is
a wonder at running through a scat-
tered field and at quick

SOUTH PASADENA BRIEFS.

SOUTH PASADENA, Dec. 22.—At
the request of the Los Angeles Gas
Company, the Railroad Commission
called a hearing before the Board of
Trustees this afternoon in the Coun-
cil chambers at 2 o'clock, for the
ratification of the franchise which was
granted to the Los Angeles Gas and
Electric Company some time ago.

Ordinances requiring that com-
panies supplying water and electric
energy to the residents of this city
furnish the city with detailed state-
ments of their expenses and their
recipts have been passed by the
Board of Trustees. The water com-
panies must furnish a detailed state-
ment of their business to the city by
January, 1914, and the electric com-
panies have been given until February,
1914, for a similar statement to be
filed in the City Clerk's These
statements are necessary before the
Trustees can fix the rates and they
will not Introduce any new feature as
the Trustees have been accustomed to
having the reports from the com-
panies.

Dr. Lottie Park, who is the exam-
ing physician of Resthaven, spoke and
interested her hearers in the work
which the Psychopathic ociety is striv-
ing to do at Resthaven. She told of
the reforms brought about recently
in the treatment of insane people, and
said that more than 250 women had
been eaved from Patton during the
last year, and sent to Resthaven,
where they recovered.

ANTA MONICA, Dec. 22.-——The

contract has been entered into for

the great automobile road races to
be pulled off over the world-famous
Santa Monica course, February 21-23.
The Vanderbilt cup affair falls on the
date first named and the Grand Prix
on the Monday following. A purse of
$15,000 is guaranteed by the Western
Automobile Association, and if the
gross receipts admit of it the award
will be $20,000. The Chamber of
Commerce and the Western associa-
tion are the parties to the contract,
the former promoting the affair and

TO RELEASE CURTIN.

FREE CHRISTMAS EVE.

(BY Fr. NIGHT WIKRE To THE TIMER)

SACRAMENTO, Dec. 22.—Anthony
Curtin, sent fo Folsom for a burglary
in San Francisco in 1905, for a term
of ten years, had nis sentence com-
muted today by the Governor o sev
en years and five months, which, will
expire Wednesday, making him a free
man Christmas eve. The Governor
took the view that the man's sentence
should be reduced because of the time
served tm the County Jalil, and the
deprivation of hts rights of an ap-
peal by the earthquake.

(BY A. P. NIGHT WIRE TO THE TIMFS.)

SACRAMENTO, Dec. 22.—John .
Burke, convicted in Sacramento in
1898 for robbery and sentenced to
a twenty-five-year term in Folsom,
had his parole extended today to a
comptete pardon by the Governor.
Burke was let out on parole five years
apo, after having served ten years of
his term.

UOTATIONS,

REAT DEPOT

Movement Proves of FINE PASSENGER STATION,

Mission Structure of Pleasing Lines
Which Will Cost Two Hundred
Thousand Dollars Is Planned for
San Diego Before the Exposition
Opens—Brief Development Notes.

Close to $200,000 will be expended
by the Santa Fe at San Diego the
coming year in the erection of a new
passenger station. This announce-
ment was made yesterday by General
„Manager Wells of that road. Work
is to begin early the coming year, ac-
cording to Wells, “providing the mon-
ey is forthcoming.”

The plans for the new station pro-
vide for a mission structure of pleas-
ing lines to occupy the present sta-
tion site and a portion of the grounds
of the existent freight depot. Wells's
announcement followed the receiving
of two sets of plans, both of the mis-
sion type, for the new structure. De-
cision between the two, which were
submitted by the engineering depart-
ment at Topeka, rests with Wells, As-
sistant Passenger Traffic Manager
Byrne and Chief Engineer Harris. A
decision is expected to be made this

“We want something distinctive ——

January divi-
Bans been passed, as well as by

* Butte Oo. ch.

are tentative and entirely dependent
„Jon the ability of the road to get the
money for the improvement.”

Not the least interesting feature in
connection with the proposed San
Diego work is the fact that President
Ripley of the road stated here more
than a year ago that this city will get
a new station “after San Diego gets
one.” As he phrased it, the need at
San Diego is greater than here, but
both cities must eventually be sup-
plied with new stations.

A civic mass meeting will be held
fm the Council Chamber at 2 o'clock
tomorrow afternoon, at which time
the employment problem will be dis-
Suse on broader lines. The City
Council, through its Finance Commit-
tee, has extended invitations to all
civic and commercial bodies and wom-
en’s clubs to attend the 8 make
suggestions and co-operate ith the
ey authorities in solving the prob-
lem and answering the claims that
there is an appreciable number out
of employment here.

The Finance Committee of the
Council was asked to devise a way of
raising the money to give work to the
unemployed. The committee decided
to do nothing in the way of asking
the people to vote bonds, but made
finauiry among the various depart-
ments and discovered that there is
considerable work at the harbor and
much in the parks that can be done.
On every available bit of work the
force will be increased to capacity and
the city will then have a visual dem-
enstration of the actual demand for
employment.

Counctiman Conwell has a scheme
which he expects will meet the situa-
tion, supposing its exists. That is to
establish a ten-hour day on all big
city improvements like the aqueduct
and harbor work, add 26 per cent. to
the budget allowance and split the
ten-hour day into two five-hour

paying the present force for
five hours, plus the half of 25 per cent.
and letting a new force step in for
the remaining half day. This, says
Counctiman Conwell, will test the
brotherly love of the work and will

Taft has outlined briefly his opposi-
tion to the recall of judges provided
for in the Constitution of Arizona, in

House Committee on Territories. His
letter was in answer to a verbal pro-
posal made by Mr. Flood several days
ago that legisiation be enacted reliev-
ing the President of the necessity fey
passing upon the Arizona Constitution,
and putting the responsibility for its
approval or disapproval up to Congress

day, that if such a resolution were
and sent to him, his approval
would practically mean an approval
of the Arizona Constitution and the
recall of judges. The President ex-
plained, however, that at present he did
not Bnow what position he mint

{ASSOCIATED PRESS NIGHT REPORT.)

GUA PRIETA (Mex.) April 13.—-
A (Via Douglas, Ariz.) During a

battle, which lasted all afternoon
and which resulted in the capturing
of this city by the rebels, commanded
by “Red” Lopez, American troops
cros#ed the border and stopped the
fighting.

The action was taken after one man
had been killed and several wounded
in Douglas. The continued firing was
endangering the lives of Americans on
United States territory. Douglas was
under constant fire for three houra.

Following are the American
and injured:

The dead: Robert Harrington, J. C.
Edwards, fighting with the insurrectos.

The injured: E. E. Crow, will prob-
abiy die; A. R. Dickson, shot through

the foot; Carlos Lennon, shot in te
leg and back; Genevieve Cole, shot
throught the arm; W. Singleton, flesh
wound in the arm.

WHO THEY ARE. |

man employed in the yards of Douglas
and was on his train at Fourth street.
A bullet struck him in the head and
he tumbled from a car. He was picked
up and taken in a Wagon to the
Copper Queen Hospital, where he died
within an hour, never regaining con-
sciousness.

RANCHERS REGAIN PROPERTY.
This afternoon the

insurrectos re-

cluding eight taken from the C.-M,
ranch, one wagon and a let of harness,
collars and other equipment, which
filled the big wagon brought over.
Three of the mules taken from the
| Cudahy ranch were killed in the en-
gagement of Saturday and two mules
and a wagon fell into the hands of the
Federal army.

The insurrectos did not, however, re-
turn the eleven saddle horses and sad-
dles taken and no offer to return the
$400 worth of supplies and stores taken
from the Cudahy § storehouse was
forthcoming.

The attention of the Mexican authori-
ties was called today to the condition
of the Inter-California Railroad and
the damage to the irrigation canals of
the California Development Company
occasioned by the practical reign of
terror imposed by the insurrectos, The
Inter-California Railroad was operated
between Calexico and Yuma in an ir-
regular fashion after January 29, when
the rebels captured the town, until
February 16, when the insurrectos dy-
namited the bridges and warned the
rallroad company to discontinue the
operation of the railroad,

After the bridges were blown out
at Calexico, General Manager A. F.
Andrade continued operating the line
between Packard and Yuma. Trains
were captured or wrecked, but Andrade
continued until the Mexican govern-
ment ordered operations stopped March
15, since which time the entire line
has been idle.

Andrade has not been allowed to
carry out plans for the reconstruction
of the part of the line destroyed. Much
damage has been done to buildings and
other parts of the property while the
rebels have been occupying the terri-

tory. ‘
While no attempt has been made to
work any damage to the canal system
of the California Development Com-
pany, the property has suffered because
of the inability to proceed with the
$20,000 expenditure necessary to main-
tain the efficiency of the system. While
no effort has been made by the in-
surrectos to prevent work on the sys-
tem, despite the best efforts of W. H.
Holabird, receiving manager of the
company, who has been in the fleld here
since the trouble started, it has been
reason of the fear of the insurrectos,
impossible to induce men to work, by
Gen. Tasker H. Bliss, commanding
the Department of California, and his
aide, Lieut. Arthur Poillon, left to-
night for San Diego by way of Los

Angeles. They will return later.

CAPTURED A TRAIN. 4
Lopez captured the Nacozari train on
its south-bound trip yesterday, and held
it near Fronteras till today, when, with
is troops abroad, numbering 150, it
| steamed back to Agua Prieta. Scarcely
had the rbels detrained when the firing
began.
| The rebels deployed their firing dine

| up and down the Nacozari railroad

tracks from the Agua Prieta station ;

to the American customhouse. With
the opening of the battle began a mad
rush of American from Douglas to-
wards the international dine, the great-
er number massing at the customhouge.
The rebels, with little rushes, their
backs bent to lower their stature undtr
fire, kept moving northwards toward
the customhouse till they were withing
its shadow. The customhouse is sur-
rounded on three sides, facing Agua
Prieta, with a veranada, which was
erowded with Americans and Mexicans
from Douglas.

One rebel attempted

to break from

rear. He
doubled up in his tracks. Another fol-

bullding, swung back out the door ans
dropped dead. Another, losing heart,
threw down his gun and broke for the
American line only a few feet away,
when Lopez leveled his gun at the
fugitive, fired, and brought him to the
earth. A faithful dog throughout thé
battle lay by this man’s side. N

The rebels swung up along the in-
ternational line, taking possession of
the Mexican guard-house, which they
made their ammunition magazine. A
group of fifteen fought from this shel»
ter, with Lopez commanding. This
house is only seventy feet from th?
une, which was toed by thousands ‘of
Americans, and the bullets spattered
in the dirt with vicious smacks. As
| the rebels swung around to this flank,

it brought the Federal fire from Agua |

Prieta directly in line with the Ameri-
can customhouse. Telephone poles
were spattered, shots dug up the sand
on all sides, but the sightseers, mad
with the enthusiasm of the fi
their ground.

ON THE MEXICAN SIDE.

Dickson, the American shot through
the thigh, had taken a position behind
a little dirt embankment to the south
of the Nacozari station, on the Mexi+
Can side, with a station employee:
Both waved their white handkerchiefs
at a squad of Federals which had de-
ployed to the east end of Agua Prieta;
but the sign of peace was answered
by a volley of shots, one of which
Struck Dickson as he
ground. A cry arose in the rebel
ranks. A daring squad of Federals
charged to the rim of the town, and
the rebels, wavering, fell back to a
group of adobe buildings. The Fed-
erals gained a building almost with-
in speech of the rebel ranks, but
thousands of shots poured into this
building, and it was deserted, leaving
its dead on guard. |

With another rush, a squad of reb-
els cashed up the boundary line, tak
ing possession of a second guard-house’
by the international monument, where
they hoisted their red, white and
green national flag, as they had done
at the magazine.

Over against the sky, standing alone
on the tallest of the adobe buildin
the comisario’s headquarters, first one,
then two courageous Federal officers,
erect, calmly noting the rebel move-

SACRAMENTO, April 13.—Declaring
that the unreasogable and extortionate
charges of transportation companies
and the Wells-Fargo Company in Cal-
ifornia, are responsible in a great
measure for the high cost of living

has the power to change them.
showed that in many instances the
Welis-Fargo Company in California
is charging as much or almost as
much for carrying articles from one
city to another, as is charged for

York City to
Governar said:
The information that has been fur-
nished to use regarding Wells-Fargo
rates shows charges within the State
of California to be higher than almost
any other place in the United States.
The most significant thing in the com-
parison of rates is in the compartson
of packages weighing six pounds or
less, between San Francisco and Los
Angeles, and New York and San Fran-

“The ‘following shows the charges

packages between New York and San
Francisce, and between San Francisco
and Los Angeles:

“New York to San Francisco, one
pound, oe; two pound, 350; three

ment, and steamers, mills and factories

The people im the launch boarded
the Northwestern and she steamed to
her wharf, which was crowded with
people. After landing passengers, the
Northwestern proceeded to Tacoma.

Tonight's cargo is considered by min-
ing men to be the most Important
shipment from Alaska since July 17,
1897, when the steainship Portiand ar-
rived here with a load of gold dust
from the Klondike placers. The ore
in the Northwestern is from the Bonan-
za mine at Kennecott, the terminus of
the Copper River Rallroad, and con-
sists of 1100 tons, valued at $225,000,
in sacks.

The ore is 72 per cent. copper, con-
taine $25 of silver per ton, and a trace
of gold. The ore is on the way to
the Tacoma smelter for reduction.

The copper mountain is said to be
all as rich as this shipment. When
the mine is further developed the ore
will receive first treatment at Ken-
necott and the concentrates will be
shipped to Tacoma for.smelting.

of State Benson. :

[RY DIRECT WIRE TO THE TIMES.)

SALEM (Or.) April 13.—[{Exclusive
Dispatch.] Dr. R. Lee Steiner. super-
intendent of the Oregon Asylum for
the Insane, left hurriedly for Red-
lands, Cal., last night. No reason for
his leaving was given out, but it is

that the condition of Secretary of

become extremely grave.
Politically, Dr. Steiner and Secre-

ment with the present State board to

FIRE IN JEROME.

[ASFOCIATED PRESS DAY REPORT.
JEROME (Ariz.) April 13.—Fire early

today caused a loss of $40,000 in the
destruction of the large stables atid
warehouse of the T. F. Miller Company
mercantile establishment and a cottage
belonging to the United Verde Copper
Company. Eight mules and five horses
were burned to death. Only the efforts
of the local fire department prevented
a very disastrous fire. The cause of the
blaze is unknown.

PEN FOR WHITE SLAVE DRIVER.

Portland (Or.) Man Canvicted for
Bringing Woman North From Los
Angeles for Immoral Purposes.
{BY DIRECT WIRE TO THE TIMES. !
PORTLAND (Or.) Apri! 13.—-[Exclu-
sive William E. Dunlap.
restaurant man and violator of the
white-slave law, was convicted before
a jury in the Federal Court today
for the alleged transportation of Mrs.
Anna Renfro from Los Angeles to
Portland for illegitimate purposes.

In his cross-examination by Deputy
United States District-Attorney Ma-
Guire, Dunlap said that, after arriv-
ing In Portland, the woman gave him
her money to keep. He told of nu-
merous expenditures he made and said
he had only $14 when he came to
Portland. During the three weeks be-
fore his arrest in February he did not
work, he said.

He admitted he first met = Mrs.
Renfro in Denver, where she was led
to leave her husband. They went from
there to Cheyenne, Wryo., he said:
thence to Hot Springs, thence to Salt
Lake City and thence to Los Angeles,
where they remained for three months.

Earl Busse and J. A. Winn, Les An-

geles policemen, testified at th¢ trial
as to the conduct of Dunlap and Mrs.
Renfro while in Los Angeles, and

their testimony was a strong factor
in securing Dunlap's conviction.

RAILROADS TO PAY TAXES.

More Than Million Dollars Due to
Flow Into State's Coffers Within
Few Days—Delinguent April 21.

[BY DIRECT WIRE TO THE TIMES.)

SACRAMENTO, April 13.~-[Exelu-

sive Dispatch} Within a few days

more than a mimon dollars will be
turned into the State treasury by the
railroad companies, the amount rep |
resenting the last installment of their

State taxes. The taxes are already

due and will become delinquent after

April 24. This will be the last pay-

ment to be made by the railroads un-

der the old system of taxation. All
subsequent payments will be in ac-
cordance with the provisions of the

Curtin bil, which puts the new Syn-

tem of pubne service corporations tax

into effect.
Board

Members of the State of
Equalization are now at work on re
ports which are being submitted by
the various railroad companies, and
hope to he able shortly after May 15
to fix the rates of taxes under the new
scheme.

SLOPE BRIEFS.

Saplo Was Not Sapicnt.
SACRAMENTO, Apri! 13.—Antonio
Sapio, wanted in Chicago for the forg-
ery of a check for $2000, was arrested
here today in the postoffice. Sapio had
been traced from Chicago to the Coast
by a detective agency. A special serv-
ice man Was went from San Francisco
to watch for Sapio. Sapio was ex-
pected to appear in the postoffice to get
mail through the general delivery, To-
day he did appear and was captured.

Attorney Healy then read an affidavit
from Frank J. Russell. This affidavit
stated that Hines had declared “we
put Lorimer over and it cost us a lot
of money, but he is well worth all
of it to us.”

The affidavit further stated that this
conversation resulted from a discus-
sion of the tariff on lumber.

DAMAGE IN SHASTA,

(BY DIRECT WIRE TO THE TIMES.)

REDDING, April 13.—(Exclusive Dis-
patch. ] The cold weather last night
and the frost next morning did tremen-
dous damage to orchard fruits and gar-
den vegetubies in Shasta founty. There
Was no frost this morning though the
weather continues unusually cold for
April. In the great prune belt around
Anderson at least halt t prospective
crop has been destroyed, meaning a
loss of $200,000 to the farmers. Peaches
were badly nipped and there won't be
half a crop of grapes.

W. R. Sheppard, own
yard two miles east of Redding, says
all his grapes are killed for this year.
On Stillwater, northeast of Redding.
peaebes were frozen on the trees. Peas,
tomatoes and other tender garden veg-
etables are completely destroyed and
